paragraphs.text: Again: the Plerophoriae, that is, the testimonies and revelations that came from God to the saints concerning the heresy of the two natures and the transgression that took place at Chalcedon, written by one of the disciples of the holy Peter the Iberian, whose name is the priest John of Beth Rufina, of Antioch, bishop of Maiuma of Gaza.

1. Our blessed father and bishop, Abba Peter the Iberian, used to tell us this. Before he renounced the world, while he was still in Constantinople, Nestorius was still alive and held the episcopate. The commemoration of the Forty holy Martyrs was being celebrated in the church called "the Lord's," and Nestorius rose to preach before all the people. I was present myself. He had a weak voice, though a clear one. In the middle of his sermon he began to blaspheme, saying: "Do not boast, Mary, as though you gave birth to God. For you did not give birth to God, O excellent one, but to a man, the instrument of God." As soon as he said this, a demon came upon him at that very moment [?], so that his face and his right hand were twisted backward. As he writhed and was about to fall, the deacons and ministers caught him up, carried him and brought him into the diaconicon. From then on most of the people of the city withdrew from communion with him, especially those in the palace. I did so too, before all of them, even though I had loved him dearly.

2. The same father also used to tell us about the blessed Pelagius of Edessa, a man of excellent conduct, a monk and a prophet. When he heard the blasphemies of Hiba, bishop of Edessa, he rebuked him openly and suffered much at his hands. Driven out, he came to a place in Palestine and lived there in stillness. Juvenal was still alive then, before the synod and the betrayal of the faith. Grace dwelt in him so fully that he was filled with the spirit of prophecy and was often granted visions. He used to visit Abba Peter, who was then living in stillness in the laura of Maiuma of Gaza, because the two of them loved each other greatly. One day, as he walked with the father in the solitary places of the laura, talking about the thoughts and the excellences that are in God, he said that he had been in ecstasy. Seven years before the synod he had seen the betrayal that the bishops would commit at Chalcedon. He even spoke the name of the wicked emperor Marcian, in whose days and by whose hands it would come about, and told the rest step by step. And he said: "For you and for me too, Father, that time will come, when we will be persecuted with all the saints who refuse to give in to the betrayal of the faith, and in that persecution we will end our lives." And in the end that is what happened.

3. This same Abba Pelagius was a prophet, as our father used to tell us. Once, while he was with the old man along with other saints, he had another vision before the synod and began to say, weeping: "Woe, Pulcheria! Woe, Pulcheria! Woe, Pulcheria!" We pressed him very hard to reveal what he meant. He said that Pulcheria had vowed her virginity to God and had cast out Nestorius, and all the saints everywhere used to write to her as a holy virgin who stood up for orthodoxy. Yet she would betray both the faith and her virginity and crush the saints. And this also happened. She broke the vows of chastity she had made to Christ and was joined to Marcian. So she became heir to his empire, to his wickedness, and to the torments that are kept for him.

4. Here is another story of this same Pelagius the presbyter, as told by Pamphilus, deacon of the church of Jerusalem, who was his friend. Once he went with him to pray at the holy place of Golgotha while it was still night, for that was his custom. As he stood praying he was caught up into a vision. Seized with grief and tears, he began to say: "Juvenal! Juvenal! Juvenal!" Afterwards, when he came out of the vision, the deacon Pamphilus fell before him in private and asked him what the vision was, and why he kept crying out "Juvenal" without stopping. He said: "Juvenal: if you live, you will see him escorted in this way by Romans and demons, just as you now see Juvenal escorted by monks and clergy."

5. Seeing in the spirit what was to come, this same man used to say to the holy father Peter and to the blessed John the Eunuch: "Study the divine Scriptures, my sons. And when Christ entrusts his churches to you, pray for me." In this he was foretelling the laying on of hands that would come upon them. The blessed Abba Peter was astonished and was not pleased by what was said, for he fled even the name of ordination. Troubled, he said to the old man: "You do not know what you are saying, old man." But Pelagius smiled and said: "I know what I am saying. And whoever wants to be troubled, let him be troubled."

6. At the time of the betrayal of the faith this man prayed this prayer constantly: "My Lord God, keep me from betraying the orthodox faith to the end, and from entering into communion with those who wronged the faith at Chalcedon. Wherever you will and however you will, take my spirit, even in a tavern or in the street. Only keep me from betraying it." And that is what happened. At Ascalon there was a certain Cyril, a tavern-keeper of orthodox faith, who had been driven out of Maiuma for his orthodoxy and had moved to Ascalon, where he kept a tavern. The blessed Pelagius was fleeing and hiding with him at night, and there he died, in keeping with his prayer and his prophecy. Some of the zealous brothers of Maiuma learned of it and came by night. They took his body and buried it in the laura, in the monastery of Aaron the lover of Christ, the wheat-seller. On the very night he died, the orthodox bishops were being persecuted, and Abba Peter the bishop had moved away and was at Oxyrhynchus in the Thebaid, a great distance away. There he saw the blessed Pelagius in a vision, coming to him joyfully with a cheerful face. He greeted him and said: "Father, pray for me and send me on my way quickly, for I am going to the Lord." The father noted the day on which he saw the vision, and later he found that it was the very day on which the great confessor Pelagius had died. His mother conceived him in holiness while she was keeping a week's fast [?], and she bore him and raised him. When he grew up and came of age, one of the distinguished men of the city died, and he saw him being carried to burial. He was pierced to the soul, and straight from that funeral he fled to a monastery, for he had seen the folly of this world. And so he became a chosen vessel.

7. The blessed John, presbyter of Alexandria, who was called "of the house of Tatinos" [?], a well-known and respected man, told us this: "When I was a boy, I wanted to renounce the world. I used to go to Abba Elidius the prophet, and I ran to his cell to tell him my desire and to learn from him whether the Lord would bring my longing and eagerness to completion. I begged him to pray for me. He said: 'Wait for now, for I do not see that you are ready for the monastic life yet. Go in peace, and be diligent about the way of excellent conduct. After a certain time a persecution will overtake the church. Then you will flee and come here, and become a monk.' I asked Abba Elidius: 'What persecution? Will paganism seize us?' He said to me: 'No. A wicked emperor named Marcian will arise, and he will make the bishops declare in writing that the one who was crucified is not God. All of them will obey him and give in, except the bishop of Alexandria alone, Dioscorus I mean. He will not obey him. For this he will be persecuted and sent into exile, and there he will die.' I said to him: 'Will the people of Alexandria let him go into exile?' He said to me: 'Yes. They will be overpowered, and another man, a heretic, will take his place.' I was distressed by what he said, and he went on: 'But in these days God will raise up a priest who does his will.' He was pointing to the blessed Timothy. 'And the one before him will be killed by violence.' He was hinting at the wicked Proterius. 'Timothy will remain only a few days in the episcopate and then be cast into exile.' When the old man had said this, he fell silent. I was in great distress and said: 'My lord father, will that orthodox bishop remain in exile, then? Will the city and all Egypt be lost, and wickedness prevail?' But he was silent. I waited and pleaded, and he said to me: 'Yes, there will come a time when he returns. He will remain a short time and then die in the orthodox faith.' When he had said this, he fell silent again. I fell down before him, wanting to learn from him what would come after. But he said: 'That is enough for you. From now on, after these things, it is the time of the Antichrist that approaches.'"

8. The blessed Zeno, the wanderer and prophet from Kfar Sa'arta, a village in Palestine, also prophesied this before the synod of Chalcedon to Abba Stephen the monk, who later became a deacon of Jerusalem. Stephen wanted to go into voluntary exile for God's sake and share in the excellence of the life of a stranger. So he came to Abba Zeno and asked whether the Lord would fulfil his eagerness. He heard from him: "For now, go in peace. A persecution and an uprising of heretics will soon overtake the church over the orthodox faith. Then you will go into exile without wishing to, if you want to remain orthodox." And this did happen to him: in the end he went into exile, and he died in it because of the synod of Chalcedon. It was the blessed Zeno's custom to receive all the monks who came from everywhere, to hear the thoughts of each one, and to tell each what would lead to his salvation. But at last he foresaw the evils that would overtake the world because of the apostasy at Chalcedon, and a year before the apostasy he shut himself in and no longer received anyone. He spent that whole year before the synod of the apostates in mourning and groaning.

9. Abba Innocent of Pamphylia, a chaste man and a superior of brothers, used to tell us this. In Pamphylia there is a great, deep gorge [?], and in it lived one of the holy and humble men. Once, before the synod, he saw the devil come to him and say: "Fall down and worship me." The saint breathed on him and rebuked him, and that unclean demon withdrew, saying to him: "Why have you refused to worship me? Look, I am gathering all the bishops and holding a synod, and there all the bishops will worship me."

10. What I am about to say may perhaps be hard to believe and may seem to people like a marvel. But chaste and aged men worthy of belief, and holy monks, told it to me. So did those who at that time were living in the monastery of Abba Romanus and have been honoured in his memory [?]: Abba Atrebius, a man without guile; Abba Pragmius; Abba Thomas Dogia [?], the chief disciple of Abba Romanus; and many other old men of upright conscience. They did not keep silent about a sign that took place in Palestine, which foretold the apostasy of the bishops. When the lawless synod was about to take place, the sky suddenly went dark with gloom and thick cloud, and stones rained down on the holy city, on all the villages around it, and on many places in Palestine. They were all alike in form in every respect, and they looked like stones made by human hands. They bore varied and beautiful markings, so many people gathered them. And those who used them without knowing what they were went blind. People said that Hesychius, the preacher of Jerusalem, gathered many of them, showed them to the empress Eudocia, and sent them to Constantinople as proof of the sign. It pointed to the blindness that seized the world through the apostasy of the bishops, as Isaiah the prophet said: "The servants of God have been blinded." A great deal of fine dust was seen beneath the stones, showing that they had come down from above. Some of those who lived nearby said that even now, in the village of Gitta, a basket full of them is kept. Our blessed father Peter bore witness to these things too. He said that in those days he heard clearly about this sign from those who had seen it, while he was living in stillness in the monastery of Maiuma. And Abba Andrew, his disciple, confirmed that he had seen three such things with his own eyes. The first was this sign of the stones. The second was a man who had long been blind, who appeared to him after his eyes were healed by the blood of the holy monks killed at Neapolis at the time of the apostasy. The third was the offering that openly became blood and body in the church of the Apostles at Caesarea. The holy orthodox fathers had gone out to meet Juvenal the apostate as he returned from the synod, to reproach him or persuade him to repent and set himself right. The governor stopped them from entering Caesarea, because they were a great crowd. A great crowd also streamed out to them and urged them to celebrate the offering in the church of the Apostles, which is outside the city. Many believers took some of that offering and kept it at home, and afterwards they found it to be real flesh and blood. Abba Maxus the presbyter, a man worthy of trust, also bore witness to this marvel, saying that he himself had witnessed this mystery. If anyone does not believe in this marvellous sign of the stones, let him learn of something similar that happened at that time, which everyone acknowledges and which is attested in a public document, and let him accept the truth. On the very day that the wicked Marcian ascended to the throne and put on the crown, darkness suddenly seized the whole world, with gloom and falling sand, a darkness like the one that seized Egypt. The air grew so dark that all the inhabitants of the imperial city were everywhere in great fear and turmoil. They mourned and cried out loudly and lamented, as though the end were coming quickly. This was a prophecy of the darkness that was going to come upon the whole world at the tyrant's hands, and of the blindness and darkening of the fear of God. The whole creation, so to speak, mourned beyond words and foretold the apostasy from God that was taking place, and the oppression of the orthodox faith by the wicked emperor and by so vast an assembly of the bishops of the world. That darkness lasted until evening. And the proof, testimony and full assurance of these things, beyond any doubt, does not come from outside. It comes from the very documents of the tyrant who fought against God, which he published openly. He saw the turmoil and the mourning [?] of the soldiers and of the whole city, and that everyone was taking his reign as an omen that it would bring great evils upon the whole world. He was afraid and in great turmoil. So he first issued public documents in which he made a pretence of the wrath from God and explained it away to deceive the peoples. He declared the opposite, as that document teaches anyone who comes across it: "It is right for the whole world to expect an abundance of great blessings from my reign. The darkness of the emperor before me is being driven away, as it receives the light of the beauty of my rule." And this was the beginning and first of his decrees. This document was published throughout the whole world. For those who have ears to hear, eyes to see and a heart to understand, it is a reproof and an exact proof. It is an abiding record of the betrayal and estrangement from God committed by the bishops of Chalcedon, which his tyrannical zeal brought about at once and without hindrance.

11. Another sign like this took place in those days in Jerusalem, foretelling the wrong that would be done against God. For many years the precious cross had shone and glittered on the holy church of the Ascension, and it was a large one. Suddenly it was struck by fire and hurled to the ground. This shook the hearts of all who feared God. So, to console the people and at their request, the God-fearing empress Eudocia had one made of bronze in its place. It can still be seen shining today, and it contains six thousand pounds of bronze.

12. Once Abba Peter the bishop had a conversation with Abba Isaiah, who lived in stillness at the Endekation of the Dodekaton [?]. Our brothers Zachariah and Andrew, Abba Peter's cell-companions, were present, and they used to tell us what Abba Isaiah said. He said: "I remember that once I went to one of the great saints, Abba Paul the Theban. He was already old, around a hundred and twenty years of age. I heard this prophecy from him: 'After twenty years the bishops will commit a betrayal, which is the estrangement from God that the apostle foretold. It will happen through a wicked man who will become emperor, whose name is Marcian. This emperor will die after six years and a little more. After him there will be a man who will bring things to light [?] for a short time, make a partial peace in the churches, and then cease. And so troubles will press on, one after another, until the coming of the Antichrist.'"

13. Equal to this prophecy and in full agreement with it is the one given by Abba Zeno, who was called "of the Third Cell." He lived in stillness at the Enaton of Alexandria, as the great scholasticus Epinetes [?] related. He said: "When I was in Alexandria, still a boy and studying there, it was my practice, out of faith, to visit the old man often. Once I went to him as usual and suddenly stood at his cell. I saw him sitting with a rope wound in his hands and his eyes fixed upward. I thought he was praying, so I waited a little for him to finish his prayer. But he remained a long time without moving. I thought to myself that God had revealed my sins to the old man, and that this was why he did not speak to me or receive me kindly. I waited a little longer, but the old man stayed in the vision, so I turned as if to leave. Then he cried out to me in a loud voice: 'Why are you leaving?' I knelt and bowed to him. Without saying anything else to me, he said: 'Go, write this down.' At that time the blessed orthodox Timothy, chief of the bishops, was in exile. The old man said: 'After a certain number of years the blessed Timothy will return from exile and establish orthodoxy. After two years he will die, and after him his archdeacon will become bishop. In his days a schism will arise in the churches that cannot be healed until the coming of the Antichrist.'"

14. Abba Paul, who had been a sophist and lived with Abba Andrew the old man and prophet, a hard-working and truthful man, also told us this. Before the synod there was one of the great saints of Egypt who had a vision. He saw a large assembly of bishops heating a furnace to a fierce blaze. They threw into it a beautiful infant who shone like light, and sealed the furnace with plaster on every side, so that not even smoke could be seen coming out of it and no air could get in. After three days he saw the infant come out of the furnace unharmed, and he knew that it was the Lord. As someone who was used to speaking with him, he said to him: "Lord, who are these who did this to you and threw you into the furnace?" He answered: "Bishops have crucified me again, and have plotted to rob me of my glory." And he spoke well, for the disease of the Jews afflicts the Nestorians, who call the one who was crucified a mere man and not God made flesh. As the old man looked again, he saw an old man standing far off. He did not agree with those other bishops or take part with them, neither when they heated the furnace nor when they threw the child in and sealed it up. The old man said to the child: "Who is this old man?" He said: "That is Dioscorus, chief of the bishops of the Alexandrians. He alone did not share in their plans." Then the old man, like one who had gained boldness, took courage and said to the Lord: "My Lord, how is it that the bishops of Alexandria so often fight to the death for the truth?" He said: "It goes back to the time when Simon of Cyrene carried my cross. Cyrene is part of Egypt. From then on it was foreknown in prophecy that Egypt, of which Cyrene, lying in Libya, is a part, would carry my cross to the end, stand by me, and show zeal for me to the death."

15. To confirm and fully assure this, we must add to our account what I heard from a man who went into exile with the blessed Timothy and was present at the saint's death, and who repeated his very words. He used to relate that when the blessed Timothy was about to die, he called the leading clergy and said to them: "Even if I become a fool, as the blessed apostle said, I still think it necessary, for your caution and knowledge and for your assurance about the time that has come, to tell you something that happened to me when I was a small boy going to school in the morning. I will tell you. A certain old man met me, gracious, chaste and worthy of God. He embraced me, put his hands on my head and kissed me, with a bright and radiant face, and said to me: 'Peace to you, Timothy, bishop of the end.' When he had said this three times, he vanished. And I never saw him again."

16. Once, when I was living in Jerusalem, I made a journey along the road that leads from Siloam across the valley to the places beyond it. With me as a guide was a well-known man, one of the inhabitants of the city, who knew those places. Looking to the left side of the road, I saw beneath the mountain there a large monastery, decayed and fallen down. Around it were various trees, some dried up and others gone wild, and its vineyard had turned to thorns, as though it were worthless. Astonished, I said to my guide: "I wonder how, when all these foreigners come to Jerusalem and are so eager to find places, to buy them and build monasteries and hermitages for themselves, this place has been left uninhabited and become a ruin. Who does it belong to?" He smiled and said to me: "This monastery was Juvenal's. He was living in stillness in it when he came to the episcopate. Since the synod of Chalcedon took place, it has fallen into ruin beyond all reason, as if struck by a blow of God's wrath. As you see, this place has collapsed and is uninhabited and wholly desolate, and no one is able to live in it." Astonished and groaning at the same time, I said: "Truly Juvenal was a companion of Judas, as the blessed Dioscorus said of him. That is why this place has inherited the curse of Judas. For about him the Scripture inspired by the Spirit says: 'Let his dwelling be desolate, and let no one live in his tents.'"

17. I also remember hearing this from our father Abba Peter, along with many others. During these days of the holy Forty, Juvenal used to make the rounds of the monasteries around the holy city and visit those who lived as ascetics in them, according to an old custom. He came to an old man, one of those ancient and great ascetics who were close to God. When the old man learned that he was coming, he held fast the door of his cell, bolted it, and kept quiet inside. Juvenal arrived with the crowd of city clergy surrounding him, and they knocked at the door, but he did not open. They kept waiting, and were determined either to climb down from the roof or to break the door. Then the old man began to shout: "Antichrist, go away from me! I will not let the Antichrist enter my cell! Judas the traitor will not come in here!" And he said many other things of the same kind. Those who were with Juvenal were both angry and ashamed at what was said. But Juvenal said to them: "Leave him alone. He is out of his mind. Too much asceticism has dried up his brain, and he does not know what he is saying." This was proclaimed throughout the whole city and the surrounding country. Everyone who heard it waited to see what would happen, for they knew that old man to be a holy man and a friend of God, full of spiritual grace, who never said anything idly.

18. Another thing like this happened as a sign in those days, as our father Peter told us. He was still living in Jerusalem at that time and saw what happened. He said that in the church called the Probatica, the place of washing, where the Lord healed the paralytic, there was a young reader, one of those appointed there. One day, while he was on his day of duty and serving in that holy place, he saw our Lord and God Jesus plainly, entering in glory with a company of saints. The Lord saw the lamps of the church, some of them gone out and others burning poorly. He cried out and said: "What am I to do with these people? I lavish such good things on them, oil and wine and everything else they need, and they never lack anything, and yet this only gives them an excuse to be careless and to despise my service. Woe because of Juvenal! He has made my house a den of robbers and filled it with harlots, adulterers and drunkards." As he said this, he went into the diaconicon and ordered the chests containing the holy vessels to be opened. When he saw that these too had been neglected, along with other things of the same kind, he cried out and said to those who were with him: "Take them, wash them well, sprinkle chalk on them, and set them in order properly." When this had been done and he was coming out of the diaconicon, he saw the reader, who was cowering and trembling with fear. He said: "And what is this one doing here? Put him out." The reader fell on his face and said: "Have mercy on me." The Lord said to him: "Get out of here. I do not know your works." But he stayed there pleading, and the Lord said to him: "Will you repent from now on and give up your carelessness?" He answered: "If your mercies help me, I will do as much as I can." Then the Lord withdrew. From that day the reader remained in amazement and boundless grief, seized by groans beyond words. When day came, the ministers of that church and the people of the neighbourhood came running. Seeing him so full of grief and so agitated, they asked him to tell them why. He boldly told them the whole vision he had seen, and the holy vessels themselves bore out what he said. For when they opened the chests, they found the vessels shining with a divine radiance. Instead of chalk, something like dust had been sprinkled on them, strange and worthy of wonder, with a strong and delightful fragrance. When this became known throughout the city, crowds rushed to the place. I myself went with my brother John, of blessed memory, and we became witnesses of this marvel. But when Juvenal heard of it, he could not bear the shame and the reproach of what was being said about him, for it was no trivial matter. By night he took away the man who had seen these things and made him disappear. How, and where, God knows. The blessed Peter also used to say that he knew one of those blessed men who lived in stillness in the holy city, though he did not make clear whether he was speaking about himself or about someone else. He said he knew a man who, in the days of Juvenal, had a vision in which he saw the defilements that were taking place inside the holy house. From that day on he refused to go into church with him or to receive the offering from his hand, but used to receive it privately in the diaconicon. This was before the betrayal at Chalcedon had taken place. But he did not tell us who this saint was who saw the vision.

19. Our blessed father, the man of God, used to add this to the story. He could not bear the abominations committed by Juvenal, his kinsmen and his attendants, and he saw many people stumbling. And, as it were because of the great number of pilgrims who were coming there from every place, and as if by divine inspiration, he shut himself up alone in a cell from the ninth hour. There he poured out his soul before God with bitter tears and mourning, kneeling and standing again and again. Then, as though filled from the very presence of God, he said: “What ought I to have done for human beings that I have not done for their salvation? I established the heavens. I spread out the earth. I planted paradise. I made the whole creation serve their delight. After Adam’s transgression I gave the law. I sent patriarchs and prophets. I worked a multitude of signs and wonders to persuade them. And at last I sent my only-begotten Son for their sake. When he came to them he proclaimed the kingdom of heaven. He granted forgiveness of sins. He healed their sick. He made the blind see and the lame walk. He drove out demons. For their sake he was crucified, and for their sake he died. He abolished death, rose from the tomb and confirmed the hope of the resurrection. When he ascended to heaven he sent the Spirit. He sent out apostles and evangelists. He overthrew the idols. And in return for all this they wrong me and my laws, trample on my commandments and transgress against my faith. See, their house is left to them desolate.” After this vision he did not stop. Every day, whenever he finished that same service, he would offer the same lament alone for a long time, with tears and with words like these. This went on until the time of the transgression at Chalcedon was drawing near.

20. Gantha is a village fifteen miles from the holy city, lying to the north. It once belonged to the empress Eudocia, but now it is part of the endowment of the church of Jerusalem. In it lived a priest from the village itself named Paul. From his youth he loved the monastic life, and he was adorned with every virtue of the Gospel: holiness, virginity, chastity, love for the poor and love for strangers. All the people honored him, and so did the empress, and he was chosen before God. In that village he founded a coenobium, that is, a large and handsome monastery, and he was father of a great community of monks. In the end the villagers seized him and he became priest of the village church. People who knew the man from experience affirm that in all those years, while he ministered to the village, men and women alike, he strove, along with his other virtues, never again to look on a woman’s face. When the lady Eudocia learned this and found it true by experience, she received communion from him alone until her death and from no one else, whether bishop, cleric or even monk. Our blessed father Peter also bore witness to this man’s virtue in God, for he loved him dearly and was closely bound to him.

When the synod of the wrongdoers at Chalcedon was already being assembled, this blessed Paul had a vision in the night. He saw a great plain that held, so to speak, the whole of humanity. In the middle of the plain he saw a high hill, and on top of the hill a ciborium resting on pillars of gold and silver. Beneath it stood an altar adorned with precious stones and fine pearls and giving off indescribable rays of light. Around it stood a great company of saints who ministered at the altar, and some of them, he said, he knew to be still living at that time. A voice came from heaven saying: “Anathema to anyone who says two natures!” Only those standing around the altar answered with a loud voice: “Amen.” But the multitudes that filled the plain stood silent in fear and trembling, astonished. Again the divine voice cried out: “Anathema to anyone who divides the One who is indivisible! Anathema to the unbelievers!” And again only those around the altar answered: “Amen.”

When the vision ended, the old man was at once seized by great distress and groaning. He wondered and pondered whether something leading to stumbling had come about through the synod of Chalcedon and through Juvenal. For that impious man had also called at Paul’s coenobium on his way up to Constantinople. Juvenal honored him, because he saw that the empress Eudocia had great faith in him. He had said to the old man: “I have stopped to see you because I may never be able to see you again. We are going up to a contest, and exile lies before us, unless we trample on our conscience toward God. For they are demanding that we do wrong and deny the faith of our fathers, and that we let the ideas of Simon the sorcerer and of the Jews prevail, as though Christ, who suffered for us, were not God. So pray for me, my lord father, that I may not be put to shame in my old age.”

The old man remembered these words and kept pondering and wondering over the vision, and he could find no answer. Then he again saw in the night Juvenal himself, standing in a corner, naked and trying to hide out of shame. He was blackened all over like a brand from a furnace, with a bridle clamped on him, [?] and covered in patches. The old man cried out to him in a loud voice: “My lord archbishop, who has done this to you? What does this garb you are wearing mean?” He answered: “What shall I do about my sins? Look, you see my shame. I am gathering a great deal of gold for the Antichrist, because he is going to wage war against the dust.” When the old man got up, he was astonished at the vision and reflected that nothing good had come from the synod, only stumbling. He waited for the outcome to confirm the truth. And when the denial was proclaimed everywhere, the old man marveled at the vision he had been given. He also tried to understand what Juvenal had meant in the vision when he said that the Antichrist would wage war against the dust. Enlightened by the Holy Spirit, he understood that “against the dust” plainly means against human beings, who were formed from dust and earth. All who are of the dust and held fast by earthly things, the Antichrist will seize and overcome and lead astray.

21. From here I am compelled to tell a fearful and terrifying story to confirm the truth, with the true God as my witness. I had direct experience of it, for I heard it, without any doubt, from those who saw the truth for themselves, and I have no doubt about it.

There is a city in Isauria called Titiopolis, because it was built some time ago by the emperor Titus. Its bishop was a man named Pamprepius, a chaste man, whose coenobium was Archis, that is, the chief monastery of that region. He was taken from the coenobium by force and received the priesthood of that city. When the synod was held at Chalcedon, Basil, metropolitan of the city of Seleucia in Isauria, took this man with him to the synod along with other bishops. When Pamprepius arrived at the synod, he saw how the great body of bishops struggled for the truth at the beginning. For practically all of them anathematized those who said two natures, accepted the blessed Dioscorus, and would not accept the Tome of Leo or those who had been justly deposed: Flavian, Ibas and Theodoret. Then he saw their fall and their denial afterward. Dioscorus, who had fought for the truth, was cast out by them, while the heretics who had earlier been condemned and who fought against God were received back without trial and against the canons, and took back their sees. At this he went back to his lodging. He shut himself in and kept vigil with tears and groans, crying out to our Lord: “God of truth and Savior of the worlds, true light, my hope from my youth, do not abandon your servant. Do not let me fall away from my hope in you and become a denier and an apostate in my old age. Make your will known to me. I am a simple man, and many pretend to the truth. So reveal to me, by your unerring judgment, whether what has been done at this synod is according to your will, and who is acceptable to you: Dioscorus, archbishop of Alexandria, whom they have cast out, or those others, who received those condemned wicked men without trial and endorsed the Tome of Leo. Then, assured by your goodness, I may stand firm in the truth, without doubt, until death, and not transgress against the faith of my fathers and the hope I have in you.”

He spent three days and nights like this, kneeling before the Lord and pleading. Then he saw this vision. A great scroll of paper was stretched out from heaven and came down to the earth. On both sides of it, front and back, was written in large letters: “Anathema to this synod! They have denied me, they have denied me! Anathema, anathema!” After he saw this vision he was fully assured, without doubt. That very night he left everyone behind, slipped away and went to his city. When he arrived there, he gathered all the people of the city. He told them everything that had happened at Chalcedon, how the bishops had denied orthodoxy, and how he had received assurance from heaven about it. He solemnly declared to them: “This is why I hurried to get here ahead of the others and make the truth known to you, so that no deception or error may overtake you. If you are ready to stand firm with me, unshaken in the orthodox faith, if you will hold fast to me and flee from these deniers and their communion, then I am ready to stay with you and to struggle for your salvation until death, and, if need be, to lay down my life for you. But if you are inclined to enter communion with Basil the metropolitan and those who think as he does, I am innocent of your blood, and I will free and save my own soul.” In this way he set their hearts on fire with love for God and zeal for the truth.

After this he remained in the episcopate for seventeen years. He kept his flock in blameless purity, without any departure from the orthodox faith, even though he was severely tried by dangers and plots from Basil, metropolitan of Isauria, and from the man who was called patriarch of the city of Antioch, for they were supporters of the heterodoxy of Chalcedon. But under God’s protection and grace he persevered, without slackening, wavering or turning aside. He guarded his flock, and so he departed gloriously to God his Savior, Christ, having woven the crown of confession. Now I must, for the assurance of those who hear, tell how this assurance came to me.

22. Peter, who became archbishop of Antioch in the time of the Encyclical, and from whom I, unworthy though I am, received the priesthood, returned from exile to Antioch and took up the high priesthood. He then sent his synodical letter to the administrator of the holy church of God in Jerusalem, who at that time was Martyrius. He sent it by the hand of a man named Peter, a bishop, who was Isaurian by birth and came from the Titiopolis mentioned above. He governed that see as the disciple, attendant and heir of the most excellent and blessed confessor, Bishop Pamprepius. For he was thought worthy to receive that man’s high priesthood, and it was expected that he would show zeal equal to his for the orthodox faith. Along with him was sent a priest of the church of Antioch named Solomon, Armenian by birth, who had once been a fellow attendant with my lowliness and was very fond of me. Peter ordered them to persuade my feeble self by every means to come back to him.

For after his exile and the seizure of the city of Antioch by heretics, I had left and been granted the company of the holy fathers in Palestine. Above all there was my father, who presided over me and received strangers, Abba Peter the Iberian, the bishop, and also the great monk Abba Isaiah. After I had richly enjoyed the fruit of this saint, I resolved to live from then on in Palestine and not to be parted from their faith, their hope and the benefit they gave. I was living in quiet in Jerusalem, where at that time there was a large community of orthodox fathers, who had a dwelling there and cells for quiet.

When the men bringing the synodical letters reached the holy city, I mean Peter, bishop of Titiopolis, and Solomon the priest, they searched hard and found my lowliness. They pressed me eagerly and without letup, urging me and insisting that they would take me back by any means. They showed me a large amount of [?], that is, provisions for the journey, and letters from Archbishop Peter full of great joy and persuasion. To persuade me further they added: “We have orders from him, for your full assurance, to persuade you by every means to come to him. He says: ‘Only let him come to me, so that we may see each other. And give him my word that no one will force him to receive communion before he is persuaded. I will leave him in peace.’”

Without delay I made all this known to my holy father and savior after God, Abba Peter the Iberian. He was staying at that time in the places near the city of Ascalon. I pleaded with him and asked him to send me a short answer telling me what he thought best. A few days later I received from him a reply of this kind, the letter of the holy Peter the Iberian: “When we read the letter from your chastity, all of us who love you fell into mourning, sorrow and groaning. We see the snares of the devil spread out everywhere, ready to rob you of your hope and your salvation in God, and to bring to nothing the labors you have endured for your soul and for the orthodox faith. For it is clear beforehand that if you go to Antioch, you will be shaken and won over by affection and by the man who holds the see there, and either you will enter communion with him, or, if you hold back, you will be watched as an enemy. So do whatever you can, and we here are doing what we can, so that you may not [?] God, nor lose great things, nor grieve us who love you.”

When I received this answer, I made up my mind to be persuaded by the words of the saints rather than by those who lead people astray. I pleaded with our Lord and Savior, who in his mercy had brought me out of darkness and the shadow of death, that I might not be put to shame. The men from Antioch were pressing me hard and doing everything they could to take me. My household and kinsmen from Arabia came as well and joined in pressing me. When they heard the news they were delighted, being worldly and caring about worldly things, and they rushed to me at once, doing everything to move me and hurry my return to Antioch. I fled to the Lord and fell down before him without ceasing, and the holy fathers struggled alongside me in their prayers. Then a divine dispensation came about. Both men, Peter the bishop and Solomon the priest, suddenly fell into a severe and dangerous illness, the one called hemitritaeus, that is, half-tertian, a tertian fever. When I learned of their illness, it seemed fitting and right to me to visit them, although until then I had been reluctant even to be seen by anyone.

I went to where they were lodging, a fine and admirable house. I saw the bishop lying opposite the door, in convulsions. When he heard that I had come, even though he was burning with fever and convulsing, he leapt up from the bed and cried out: “Come in peace, servant of Christ!” And in a loud voice, I tell you, he said: “Have mercy on me, have mercy on me! I have sinned against you, I have sinned against you! Whether I live or die rests with you. I know for certain that I am suffering this because of you, and the wrath of God has come upon me. For this is God’s judgment: my own ruin and transgression were not enough for me, but I also called you, who stand firm, so that you would suffer the same as I and become a denier. I beg you, from this day on we will press you no more. Do as you wish, only pray for me. For you see the affliction and danger we are in, both of us, and how we have come to our last extremity.”

I was astonished and amazed at these words, and I asked what the reason was for such words and such a change. With great anguish and tears he began to tell the whole account from the beginning, which I have set down above, about the blessed Pamprepius, bishop and confessor, who had been his father and the head of his monastery. He told how Pamprepius was at the synod; how he saw from the start the bishops’ struggle for the truth, and then their betrayal and denial; how he shut himself up in his lodging and pleaded with the Lord; what assurance and revelation he was granted; how he came to his city and proclaimed the truth to them and the denial that had openly taken place; how he remained to the end unbending and no denier, and so was made perfect in glory and a fine old age. Then, with shame and tears, Peter told about himself: how he had been drawn away by desire for the episcopate, had been won over by Basil the metropolitan, had transgressed against the faith and had become a partner in the synod of those deniers.

When I heard this, I was grieved in my soul, and I understood how great God’s mercies had been toward my wretchedness. After our conversation I at once hurried to the holy Anastasis, waiting for a quiet time. I fell down before the altar and the venerable Golgotha, and with bitter tears from the depth of my heart I cried out: “Lord, who am I? A sinner and a dead dog, a worm, a house of provocation, a den of thieves, a defiled tomb. Yet you have poured on me the abundance of your mercy and your wonders, which you have multiplied and worked according to your mercies and your compassion. Those who came for this very purpose, who wanted me and were scheming in every way, pressing and urging me to become a denier and fall away from my hope in you and from a good conscience, have themselves become for me confirmation, edification and warning. What then shall I render to the Lord my God for all that you have done for your servant? So I offer you the words of David: I will give great thanks to the Lord with my mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise him, for he stood at the right hand of the poor, to save him from his persecutors.”

I have judged it right and good, and indeed very necessary, to set these two fearful and true stories before everyone, as if on a pillar. Let them make known to all who fear God and are zealous for the orthodox faith, and let them persuade them with all their soul and without doubt, that the sentence has gone forth from heaven above: the synod of Chalcedon is anathema, and so is everything done at it, and so are all who think and teach as they did.

Since I have mentioned Isauria, I think it necessary, to confirm what has been said, to add this story as well. It concerns the blessed Stephen, who was abbot of the monastery called Tagon, in Seleucia of Isauria. He was once the foremost zealot for the orthodox faith and the head of the movement that first shone out in Isauria and from there spread through the whole East. He was glorified and made perfect in this contest; he fought the good fight and finished his course, and for this he rightly received the crown.

23. The story is this. “I used to be a friend and admirer,” he said, “of Basil, who was bishop of Seleucia in Isauria. He was considered a fine and eloquent speaker. When the synod of Chalcedon assembled, he attended it too, with the other bishops of Isauria who were under his authority. Before that he was regarded as zealous and truly orthodox. But when news of the denial that took place there spread and was heard everywhere, astonishment and amazement seized everyone. People could not believe that Basil too had denied the faith and been swept along into agreement with the others, and I least of all, since I was his friend and admirer. When he came back to Isauria and was about to enter the metropolis, many hesitated and resolved not to enter communion with him until they had received full assurance about the truth. I was one of them.”

The blessed Stephen said: “I was still a layman then. I hesitated, and I prayed to God in faith and simplicity of heart to make known the truth about this to my lowliness. That very night I seemed to see Basil coming back. All the people ran to meet him and brought him into the church with honor, praise and acclamation. A great crowd was about to finish gathering, and he was standing at the altar in the presence of the whole city, women and children included. Then through the western doors of the church came a man of fearful appearance, tall and glorious. He made his way through the people and rushed at Basil, who was standing there about to finish the prayer. He thrust the finger of his right hand into Basil’s mouth, turned him toward himself, and so pulled and dragged him along. No one tried to stop him or dared to object. He took him out of the church, drove him off and threw him out.”

This was a prophecy of what was going to happen, and it has now come about through the settlement made by the holy and blessed Severus, archbishop of the great city of Antioch. For see, Basil’s name has been silenced and erased from the diptychs, and he has become rejected by God and by the saints. Let us take note of this: even though God was long patient, now, after so long a time, the fulfillment of this vision has come. Indeed, ever since the denial took place at the synod of Chalcedon, those who brought it about have been cast out and anathematized by God and by men.

The elder Stephen said: “At that time I was young and a layman, without experience in the precise meaning of the divine dogmas. I saw everyone being led astray by him, for he was skilled at whatever he said, and he gave everyone the impression that he spoke correctly while he concealed his shame and wickedness. So I too was swept along with everyone and entered communion with him. But now that I have been found worthy to know the light of the truth and to share in the Eucharist of the orthodox, I have remembered that vision, and through it I have received abundant and true assurance.”

24. He added this as well about himself. He told me, confiding it to me as to a dear friend, that some time earlier one of the servants of Christ had seen a vision concerning my lowliness. He said: “I seemed to see a large building in the form of a church. In it were many thrones, and on the thrones sat many bishops. And you,” he said, meaning me, “suddenly came in. And when I saw them sitting, I cried out and said: ‘Look, the deniers and the abominable!’ And I took a whip and drove them out and expelled them, and I overturned their thrones.” Father Stephen told me this in private and asked me to tell him what this sign might mean. I said that God knows, but that it is a fearful vision and not an empty one. As the outcome has shown, what the vision signified was the present ascendancy, in which, through him and by his hands, the orthodox faith has prevailed and the heretical bishops have been rejected and anathematized.

25. Hear also another declaration that came forth from heaven about the synod of Chalcedon. The one who heard it is its witness and herald: the blessed Romanus, whose name is celebrated everywhere. He was the head and governor of a great monastery near the village of Tekoa, which lies about fifteen miles south of Jerusalem. In it at that time there were more than six hundred monks, who were shepherded by the holy man and kept to a life of stillness.

When the denial and transgression of Juvenal, and of those who gathered at Chalcedon and were called bishops, became known throughout the whole East, the believers everywhere were united in inconsolable mourning and grievous distress, and the holy order of monks joined them in great numbers. They came out of their monasteries and ran to the father of the community, the man clothed in God, who stood before God at all times. I mean the holy Romanus. They begged him to be zealous with a zeal worthy of the Lord, after the likeness of Elijah the prophet, and not to stay silent about the faith that had been betrayed and the wickedness that had taken hold. They reminded him of what they had heard from Juvenal before his denial. When he was about to go to the synod, he had solemnly warned everyone, saying, "Whoever assents to this tome has his portion with Simon the sorcerer and Judas the traitor, and like the Jews he ought to receive circumcision."

So the great crowd of holy monks pressed him, and urged him to leave his monastery and be zealous with them, and to accept every toil for the truth. He persuaded them, saying, "Wait for me a few days, and after that come to me. Whatever full assurance the Lord gives me, that I will do." He went out of his coenobium and withdrew alone into the desert. There he spent ten days and ten nights fallen down before the Lord, wishing that His will and judgment might be revealed to him about what had happened at Chalcedon. Conflicting reports were going around everywhere: some rejected those decisions and spoke of them as evil, while others accepted them. When the ten days were over, he heard a voice from heaven saying, "Go, believe as you were baptized, in the faith of the three hundred and eighteen, and you will be saved."

Having received full assurance, he returned to his coenobium and revealed the vision to some modest and learned elders of the community. But they said to him, "These men who gathered at Chalcedon also confirm this very faith of the three hundred and eighteen, and claim to adhere to it, so to speak. Yet under the pretext of that very definition of the three hundred and eighteen, they have put into their own definition a bait and a snare that will lead many astray."

So he went alone into the desert again. He endured the same toil and humbled himself, and he besought the Lord that he might receive full assurance. A voice came to him saying, "Go, adhere to these men, and persevere in their teaching and in their perfection: Peter, archbishop of Alexandria; Gregory of Neocaesarea, the great wonder-worker; Julius of Rome; Athanasius, Basil, Gregory, John of Constantinople, Cyril, Celestine and Dioscorus." Having received full assurance, he returned to his monastery with joy.

But when he told them about these saints, he heard from them that even these deniers claim to adhere to them, while they interpret their teachings falsely and lead the simple astray. So it was right for him to ask God's mercy for a clear assurance, without any doubt, as to whether the synod of Chalcedon had been conceived wickedly or well. He went out into the desert, and he exerted himself in abstinence and in mighty struggle, praying with bitter tears and groans. He asked the mercies of the Lord for an answer that was clear and left no doubt. And it came to him in this way. At midday he saw a great tome coming down from heaven, and in it was written: "Those at Chalcedon have denied. They have transgressed, they have transgressed. Woe to them, and anathema!"

When the blessed man received this assurance from God, he was set all aflame with zeal for the truth and the orthodox faith. So in deep old age and weakness of body he left his monastery and the great community of brothers. He went with the holy and zealous monks who had come to him from Arabia and from Palestine. At first they planned to meet Juvenal on the road as he returned with great pride and pomp from the emperor and from the synod of the wicked. They meant to try with counsel, persuasive words and gentle speech to turn him from his evil purpose and bring him back to the right doctrines. But they found him impossible to persuade. He relied on a corruptible emperor, and he declared that it was better for him to please the emperor than God. So the whole assembly of saints anathematized him to his face and returned to Jerusalem.

There, so to speak, all the holy monks and lay people from every city gathered, together with the orthodox bishops who had stayed behind and not gone up to the synod. First they cast out the feeble Juvenal with a written anathema and proclaimed it publicly. After this, by common vote, they elected a zealous and pious bishop who was adorned with every apostolic virtue, the blessed Theodosius, I mean. They set him up as head, guide and shepherd in the holy city, [on the throne] of James [?], the brother of our Lord. Through him and by his hands they appointed bishops in all the cities. The peoples ran to this with great eagerness, chose with one accord, and put forward whoever pleased everyone and was adorned with orthodox faith and blameless conduct.

If anyone does not believe what has been said, let him take in hand the letter that Abba Romanus wrote to them, to Queen Eudocia. He wrote it while he was in Antioch, where he had been driven by the wicked tyrant Marcian. From it the whole truth about the matter set forth here will be fully established. For it is full of every kind of wisdom and teaching. It deals not only with the cause of what happened at that time; it also sets out the certainty of the doctrines of truth and of the incorruptible faith that has no error. It is enough for anyone who wishes and reflects to find the undoubted proof and testimony [?] of the truth, and the refutation of the transgression at Chalcedon.

26. There was a certain Aphelonius, a priest in Caesarea who gathered the divine church of the orthodox there. He was a man modest and holy in every respect, honored and esteemed by all, who suffered much and showed zeal for the orthodox faith. He used to tell this story.

While the blessed archbishop and confessor Timothy was still in exile in Cherson, Aphelonius went to visit him and to be counted worthy of his blessing. He saw that Timothy had an evil sore on his foot, of the kind physicians call cacoethes, which means "of an evil nature," and it was causing putrefaction. "So I reproached his attendants," he said, "for neglecting the old man's health. But they excused themselves, saying, 'Many times we have begged and asked him to let us dress the sore and put the proper remedy on it, but we could not persuade him. But now, my lord, the love of God is in you, and you would do well to do what you can too.' I too was suffering along with the old man. I was burning with love to embrace the feet of the saint without the brothers being present, so that it would not seem that I was doing this on their advice. I begged him, saying, 'Have mercy on me, and grant me what I ask of you.' The saint said, 'Get up. Whatever is possible and you wish, we will do.' But I stayed lying on my face and said over and over, 'I will not get up unless you grant me the favor.' The saint said, 'Do not argue. I have said once that whatever is possible and pleasing to God, I will do.'

"When I got up, I begged him to be persuaded and let me carefully do what was possible and helpful for the sore on his foot. He said to me, 'Wait now, sit and listen, and don't be contentious.' He put his finger on his eye and said to me, 'Look, what do you see here? Don't you see on the pupil of my eye something like a thick scar?' I said, 'Yes.' He said to me, 'I too would be a fool [to speak of this]. But so that you may be persuaded and stop blaming me, I am compelled to tell you how this happened to me.

"'Once, when I had risen early and was keeping vigil and finishing a short office, a man suddenly came in, fearful and agitated, black and dark. He looked just as the prophet Job depicts Satan. When the door was opened he came in upon me, holding a great tome in his hand. He at once stretched out his right hand and shook it, and he shouted, "Who is this who alone stands against my will? Who is this who does not submit to me? Take it now and raise your hand!" He was shaking and threatening, uttering terrifying threats, and he thought he would frighten me with the sound of his voice. But I took courage from the Lord and was strengthened, and I said to him, "What you say will not happen. I will not do your will. I will not fight against God and be a rebel like you. I know your weakness. You do not frighten me, and you do not terrify me with your threats and your raving."

"'At this he was enraged and seethed with anger. He was truly filled with harsh bitterness like a serpent or a dragon. He was holding that tome in his right hand, as I said, and he raised it and struck my eye with it in his rage. He caused me such bitter pain that I thought my eye had burst and fallen out. Yet even this did not happen without God's help. In the morning, when the brothers came in to me, they saw something like a drop of blood and flesh hanging from my eye and falling from it. The whole eye seemed almost extinguished, and nothing was left of its former true form. They wept and mourned, and they begged me to let them treat it with bandages and with whatever could heal such hurts. They supposed that, as often happens, an affliction like this came from a rheum or some such cause. But I did not let them. I said, "I know where this came from. So do not argue with me or trouble me. I have only one physician, the One in heaven."

"'I persevered in patience and poured out my soul before the Lord and asked for his mercies, and help came to me from him. Our God Jesus Christ himself appeared to me. He laid his undefiled hands on my eyes and healed me and gave me sight. He left me this small scar as an unerring reminder of the goodness of his good visitation, which I received. And now I know for certain that the one who brought that trial and that blow upon me is the one who, now too, by our Lord's permission, has brought this sore upon my foot. Then I believed in the Lord, and when I besought him I received health. So now too I believe without doubt that his visitation will come to me swiftly from him. So I beg your modesty to be at rest and stop blaming me about this.'"

That is the story. I have also heard it from many others who knew it for certain and from experience, and who were in the service of Archbishop Timothy. I heard it as well from one of those who were his attendants, who were gathered around him in Cherson and served him in exile.

Having learned these things by experience, the blessed Timothy rightly calls the synod of Chalcedon satanic in many of his letters and in his other writings. For it was gathered and brought about by the devil. It is the forerunner of the Antichrist, and it is the rebellion of which Paul the apostle spoke when he wrote to the Thessalonians.

27. Zeno was a soldier, the primicerius of the numerus of Dacians stationed in Alexandria. Cosmas the cubicularius sent him to Palestine to guard Abba Peter our bishop and Abba Isaiah the hermit, who lived in stillness, until Cosmas himself arrived. Cosmas was waiting to take them to the emperor Zeno, for he had been ordered to do this. When Zeno came to Palestine, he told the blessed man a story of this kind in our presence.

"A certain Peter, who was a scholarius, once told me: 'I was a great admirer of Nestorius. I used to praise the synod of Chalcedon and the emperor Marcian, and many times I stood up against those who accused them. Then one night I saw a man who said to me, "How long will you go astray and refuse to hold to the truth? Come, let me show you where the emperor Theodosius is, and where Marcian is." He showed me a place full of unapproachable light, where the blessed Theodosius was, in unspeakable glory, shining more brightly than the sun. Then he led me to another place, full of smoke, gloom and darkness, and said to me, "Do you see Marcian being strangled there?" I said, "I don't see anyone." He looked up to heaven and said, "Lord, take away a little of the gloom, so that he may see and believe." Then I saw Marcian hanging in iron chains in the midst of the fire, being strangled. And so I was convinced and became orthodox.'"

28. Cyriacus and Julius were modest monks, Cypriots by birth and worthy of belief. They told the blessed Abba Peter something they knew for certain and had been convinced of by experience.

In Cyprus there is a martyr's shrine belonging to a certain martyr whose name I do not now remember. He had been given the grace of a gift that came with these wonderful visitations. If anyone vowed to offer him a lamb or a dove, or any of the other things that are customarily offered, then even if that person lived in another place with many martyrs' shrines, he would only send the offering off from his house. It went there by itself and was found in the martyr's shrine. No one guided it, and none of those who met it on the way dared to touch it.

When the bishops returned from the synod of Chalcedon and wanted to lead the simple astray, as though nothing evil had happened, this holy martyr appeared openly on the roads to those who were coming to his shrine as usual. He solemnly warned them, saying, "I am So-and-so, the one you are going to. Do not go there, and do not have communion with the deniers. It is because of this that I have gone away from there, and I am no longer seen there."

29. Something similar happened at Sebaste in Palestine, where the whole body of John the Baptist lies. At the time of the synod of Chalcedon the paramonarius in that place was the holy and blessed Constantine, who always delighted in the sight of the Baptist. There was a place, an exedra of the martyr's shrine, set apart on its own and fenced off with screens. In it are two reliquaries overlaid with gold and silver, with lamps that never go out burning before them. One is that of the holy John the Baptist, and the other that of the prophet Elisha. A throne was set up and spread with coverings in that place, but no one ever sat on it. Every night, when the blessed Constantine rose for the vigil, he went into that exedra first. He greeted the reliquaries, trimmed the lamps, and carefully arranged that throne.

The blessed priest Eltus [?], whom we mentioned earlier, told us these things about him. He is the one who gathered the orthodox church of God in Caesarea. He stayed with the holy Constantine and became his disciple, and he said: "When I saw him caring for the throne in this way every day, I fell down before him and begged him to tell me the reason. Why did he take such care over it when no one sat on the throne? At first he was reluctant to say. But when he saw that I persisted in faith, he said, 'Almost every night, when I first open the door and go in, I find the holy Baptist sitting on the throne.'"

So the blessed Constantine enjoyed this kind of familiarity with holy John. When the wickedness took place, and Marcian drove out the bishops who had been ordained by the blessed archbishop Theodosius, Constantine was torn in his thoughts between two things. If he fled from communion with the deniers, he might be deprived of the company of the holy Baptist. If he remained, he would become a wrongdoer. So he besought the holy forerunner of Christ to enlighten his mind and reveal to him what was pleasing to God. And he saw the saint, who said to him, "Priest, do not destroy your soul for my sake and deny your faith. Go out, and keep your faith without transgression. Wherever you go, I am with you."

So he went out, and in exile he was kept blameless in a holy life and in the orthodox faith until the end. He fought the good fight and wove the crown of confession.

30. The God-fearing priest Zosimus, the stranger, a modest man, was counted worthy of the same kind of assurance and vision. He was also counted worthy to live with the blessed Abba Peter. To the end he kept the orthodox faith without transgression, and it kept him.

He had been living as a hermit at Raithou and on Mount Sinai, in communion with orthodox fathers. As he told me, he left those places and came to Jerusalem. He loved the way of life in these holy places, and he went around looking for a place suited to stillness. He came to Bethel, where the patriarch Jacob saw the ladder, and the paramonarius of that place took a liking to him. He frequently urged Zosimus to stay there, and promised to provide him with every comfort he needed. Zosimus told him openly that he could not do this, because he was fleeing from communion with those deniers at Chalcedon. The paramonarius promised again, saying that he would not cause him even one annoyance on that account. "Only stay here," he said, "live with me, and take care of this place."

Zosimus's mind was leaning toward this when he saw the patriarch Jacob in the night. He was a man with a full head of white hair, honored and venerable, wrapped in a cloak and holding a staff, and he was walking about the place. He came up to Zosimus and said, "You are orthodox and in communion with the orthodox. How is it that you want to settle here? Do not transgress against your faith for my sake. Be careful instead, and flee from communion with the deniers. You will lack nothing good, neither a place nor anything you need."

So he fled, and to the end he was kept steadfast in holy conduct and in the orthodox faith.

31. The blessed Abba Peter the bishop used to tell us about one of the saints, called Heliodorus the shepherd. He left the world and went to the mountaintops and the thickets of the Taurus in Cilicia. He chose to make his dwelling among the wild beasts, and he lived there for many years hidden from people. With extraordinary endurance he lived on the shoots of trees and the roots of the wilderness. For this reason his hair served him in place of a garment in winter and in summer.

Hunters of deer and wild animals came to those places, as they used to, and saw the saint from far off. Because of his wild appearance, they thought he was some strange beast. So they set snares and caught him, after many years of this kind of ascetic life. Now that he had become known, he could no longer keep up the life of solitude and of cleaving to the Cross. He was persuaded, or rather compelled, by the inhabitants of those places to come back into the world, and he lived in a monastery and became father of the monks.

When he was about to depart this life, he called his disciples and said to them, "Twenty-four years from now the bishops will deny the faith. When you see the beginning of this upheaval, flee to Egypt. For from there the remnant of the orthodox will be preserved, and also the [remnant] in Palestine which they will visit [?]."

And our blessed father said that he went to Egypt and found one of Heliodorus's disciples still alive and living there as a hermit, an old and holy man. "I heard these things from him," he said, "and I was convinced."

32. The blessed Abba Peter also said that he knew one of the saints who heard a voice from heaven while he was sitting in his cell, when the blessed and orthodox emperor Theodosius died. The voice said, "Behold, heaven is shaken and about to fall, and the earth is about to rot away, and it grieves no one. For the great and orthodox emperor Theodosius has died."

33. The father also used to tell us about a certain Comitinus, one of the Victores of Alexandria, who always came to him and received communion in the mysteries from him. Comitinus told him: "At the time when the wicked Nestorius was in exile in the Thebaid, the count sent me to pay the soldiers there, and I was forced to be in Nestorius's company. I heard a great many of his blasphemies. While I was with him, a man came and announced to him the news from above: a magistrianus had suddenly arrived who was to take him away. Nestorius was carried away by his imagination and was full of joy, and the wretch said, 'What? Did I say anything wicked when I said that Christ is not God, and that Mary is not the God-bearer?' With that word his tongue came loose and hung far out of his mouth. And so, eaten away, he died one day before the magistrianus arrived who had been sent for this purpose."

Abba Theodore the monk, who later became a bishop, went to that place, was there himself and confirmed it. He said and affirmed that even the earth did not accept Nestorius's body after his death, but cast it out three times. So the people who lived there were forced to wrap it in a basket and hang it on a wall.

The blessed Timothy set down an account of this in the ecclesiastical history he wrote. I intend, if our Lord permits, to include it among what is written here.

34. Potamon was one of those holy, ancient monks of Scetis. He came up from there and was living at that time in a cell in Egypt. Our father had left Palestine at that same time and was living in Egypt. He used to say of Potamon that he had such a gift against demons that he could drive them out just by sprinkling water on the afflicted in the name of Christ.

Our father heard about this blessed man, who was called Spelaris [?], and went to be blessed by him. He hid his identity so that no one would know who he was or where he came from. At that time Proterius was living in Alexandria and causing the saints many afflictions. But Potamon knew in the spirit who the father was, and as soon as he came in he said to him, "Do not be distressed, Abba Peter the bishop, do not be distressed. God will take vengeance swiftly. For the church of God is pleading on your behalf, you high priests. And this man sleeps with males, and he will die a violent death." He said this about Proterius. Three days later Proterius was killed.

35. There was a certain deacon named Basil, from Antioch by birth and one of its notable clergy. When Abba Peter was a youth living in the royal city, Basil guided him toward salvation and kindled in him the fire and the life of monasticism. The blessed man used to say of him that he left the world and took up the cross of Christ and carried it. For thirty-five years he lived alone as a hermit in the desert of the Thebaid.

At last he heard a voice from heaven say to him, "Basil, go to the inhabited world and fight for the faith. For bishops and emperors are going to deny the only-begotten Son of God." He came to the region of Lycia and found a steep place by the sea that no one ever walked on. He lived there for twelve years, keeping the same way of life and the same ascetic practices as the Abba Heliodorus the shepherd mentioned earlier. Then a ship put in there, and the sailors came ashore for their needs and found him. They made him known to the people who lived there. Now that he had become known, the people of that country persuaded him to come to the inhabited parts of Lycia. When he came, he founded two coenobia of holy monastics, one of men and the other of women.

In those days the wicked Nestorius was bishop of Constantinople and was preaching his blasphemies. Basil again heard a voice from heaven say to him, "Basil, hurry and go to Constantinople, and rebuke the wicked Nestorius, who blasphemes and denies faith in me." Without delay he came to Constantinople. He went into the church and found the wicked Nestorius standing on the bema, preaching. He rebuked him in front of all the people, saying, "You are deluded, bishop! Your teaching is wicked! Why do you overturn and twist the doctrines of the fathers?" When Nestorius persisted in his doctrine, Basil cried out, "Anathema on you, Nestorius, and on your wickedness!" After the assembly was dismissed, Nestorius summoned him before the bishops who were present there, and Basil exposed his wickedness openly.

Finally he approached the emperor Theodosius as he was passing through the market, and said to him in a loud voice, "Emperor, you were baptized into the Trinity. Why do you not confess the Trinity? For the things that Nestorius teaches are meant to overthrow the Trinity." He was seized by Flavius [?] the Thracian, who was magister at the time and a tyrant. Basil suffered greatly at his hands and was flogged and beaten. Everyone hated him, and the magister condemned him to exile. But as he was being paraded through the city, the people snatched him away and brought him into the house of the holy Euphemia. He stayed there for some time, beseeching the Lord who had sent him. He begged and implored Him not to keep silent until the wicked Nestorius was cut off, for the sake of the fear of God.

While things stood this way, there was a dispensation of providence. When the blessed emperor Theodosius went out into the market, a brick fell from above and struck him on the head, and he came near to the danger of death. He had been given up as beyond hope and was in great fear and trembling. Then one night he saw a man who said to him, "You have suffered this because of Basil, the servant of God, because you do not listen to him, though he is fighting for the fear of God." At once the emperor sent for the saint. When he had made his peace with him, he begged to learn from him what would please him, so that he could do it. Basil said, "I do not want things that please me, but things that are pleasing to God and that establish His churches. Command that a synod be held, so that the blasphemies of Nestorius against God may be refuted, and that he be deposed and cast out. This is the will of God." The emperor was persuaded without delay. He commanded that a synod be held at Ephesus, and that Nestorius be deposed and sent into exile.

36. Father Peter the bishop told us about the blessed Helena, a holy woman who gave alms and loved Christ in everything. She was the wife of Damarius, who was prefect of the praetorium. Three [?] years before Nestorius became bishop, an angel appeared to her and said, "Helena, Helena, three years from now so-and-so is going to sit as bishop in Constantinople. Watch over yourself, and do not receive communion from him." Three years later Nestorius became bishop. She never once agreed to receive him in her house, although he came to her many times to see her, nor would she share in the mysteries with him. But when she heard his blasphemies, she was stirred with divine zeal, and since she wanted to be truly convinced, she came to the church. It so happened that on that very day, while he was preaching, the blessed Basil, the deacon from Antioch whom we mentioned in the earlier chapters, came and rebuked him. From up in the high galleries she cried out in a loud voice and anathematized him, saying, "Anathema to you, Antichrist!" For she remembered the dream she had seen about so-and-so, since the dream had pointed to that heretic of the two natures. And since this has been mentioned, I must also tell how Nestorius came to his end in exile, to confirm the true dream of this blessed Helena. After he had been sent into exile at the Oasis, he was captured by the barbarians called the Mazices, became a captive, and was then released. He was no longer allowed to stay at the Oasis, but was kept in the city called Panos, which was named after that two-natured beast. He was kept there until the end, at the time that was told to us. Then, by a stroke of God's wrath, he received his sentence: his tongue was eaten away, and he died. To confirm this, I have felt compelled to place here among these writings the passage on this subject from the account composed by the blessed Timothy, chief of the bishops.

From the account that the holy Timothy, archbishop of Alexandria, wrote while he was in Gangra:

At that time, by God's permission and will, and because of many sins, it came about that our blessed king Theodosius passed away, one year after the second synod was held at Ephesus. The one who received the kingdom after him did not match him in his warm zeal for the faith. As a result everything in the Church was thrown into confusion, and from that time until now measures have gone forth that run contrary to the law made against the heretics, a law worthy of the memory of the blessed Theodosius. The God-fearing are persecuted, and every blasphemous and insolent tongue has taken the freedom to speak against Christ. Immediately after Marcian became king, he sent a tribune of the guards to Egypt to summon the wicked Nestorius, together with a certain Dorotheus, who had been a bishop and had gone into exile with Nestorius of his own free will. As some people have related, this Dorotheus was well known to the man who reigned at that time, and was his friend. The tribune who had been sent reached the Thebaid. This later became known to many, for it was not done in a corner. He found Nestorius in the city called Panos, a city of the Thebaid, where he was being held in some distress and suffering from a slight illness. It had happened that this Nestorius was seized by the barbarians from the Oasis, where the blessed king Theodosius had exiled him, and the barbarians sold him in the city of Panos to its inhabitants.
