When Andrew the comes, who was then in the Thebaid, learned of this, King Theodosius being still alive at the time, he sent word to Nestorius after he had been sold, advising him to stay and keep quiet in that fort, and not to do or say anything rash. When the man sent by the king found Nestorius sick in the city of Panos, as was said above, together with Dorotheus, he showed them the orders he had been given. He also told them, as though in secret, something concerning the Egyptians: that those who had been summoned would meet with no treachery. Dorotheus urged him to wait a little because of Nestorius's weakness, but day by day Nestorius grew worse. His tongue was loosened and hung out of his mouth while the tribune was there, and his speech became unintelligible. Each day it was treated again, and each day his tongue went on rotting away, until it became a fearful and grievous sight. So the tribune who had been sent later confirmed to many, with God as the mediator of what was said. For he related that he speedily brought in chosen physicians from all the cities, so to speak, around the city of Panos, and they could do nothing to help the sick man, because it was God, it seems, who had struck him. Through his account, and through the mediation of the physicians, the tribune made the manner of his death known to many. When Nestorius died, Dorotheus buried him in a certain place, with the tribune who had been sent present. After his death the tribune turned back and went to the court [?].

37. I also heard this from the Father, who related it while I was staying with him in Arca, a city of Phoenicia. He said: "When I was still a child, living in Constantinople in the palace, I watched over myself and lived as an ascetic. Thoughts arose in my mind about the mystery of the holy Trinity: how, while we confess one God, we believe in a Trinity equal in essence, eternal and without beginning; and whether the one who became flesh for us is one of the Trinity." He said that he was given a vision in which he saw the holy apostle Peter, who took him up, brought him to a high place, and set him before himself like a little child. Then he showed him in heaven a great light, unapproachable and incomprehensible, which had an orb like the form of the sun. And he said to him, "Behold the Father." Immediately another light surrounded that first one, resembling it in every respect, and in its midst was our Lord, depicted as a Nazarene. Again he said to him, "Behold the Son." With it was a third light, which resembled the first ones in everything, and the holy Peter said to him, "Behold the Holy Spirit: one essence, one nature, one glory, one power, one light, one Godhead, three hypostases." All three were unapproachable. Only the one in the middle bore the appearance of a Nazarene man, to show that the one who was crucified is one of the holy Trinity, and not another, God forbid! The other two were light alone, unapproachable, without form, incomprehensible and beyond imagining.

38. There was a certain Anianus, a scholasticus, chaste, modest and orthodox, as his father had also been. While he was still young in Alexandria, he was granted to receive baptism from our Father. After that he was in Cilicia. Then, while living in the royal city, he married a modest wife there, adorned with the other virtues, but not orthodox: she was in communion with the two-nature party. He urged her many times to come over to the Orthodox, but she remained unpersuaded. So he was moved with divine zeal and holy love, and wrote urgently to our blessed Father, who was in Palestine, for he received communion from him alone, asking him to pray to God for his wife, that He might draw her away from the communion of the two natures. When the saint was entreated, a providence like this took place. The blessed woman fell into a grievous illness, so that the physicians gave her up entirely. When she was near her end, she saw a vision like this. She was carried by angels to a deep place full of darkness and stench, where there were the voices of people weeping, and where there was no rest or consolation at all. From there angels took her again and brought her to another place, full of light and glory and inexpressible joy. There she saw an assembly of saints clothed in shining garments and praising God. Again the angels said to her, "These are the people with whom your husband is in communion. But those others are the ones in communion with the bishops who accept the synod of Chalcedon. So if you want to have communion with these, we will entreat our Lord for you to grant you a respite of life for one year. Get up, then, and live with your husband, holding his faith, and in his communion keep yourself from all sin and negligence. When the year is complete, we will come, take you, and place you in this place." When she recovered from her weakness, she immediately called her husband, who was sitting in mourning with many others in another room, dressed in black. He got up at once, so that those who were near him thought she had died. He came to her, and finding that she had revived, he sent everyone outside and learned from her what providence God had worked for her. Then she openly related everything in the vision, and cried out to him, saying, "What was revealed depends on you. If you want me to live and be with you, give me some of the holy communion of the Orthodox, from those with whom you are in communion." He was persuaded that it was God's will, and noted the day on which she had seen the vision. He had communion with him, which was sent to him every year by Father Peter the bishop. Trusting her and relying on her, and since she had been the first to ask for it, he gave her some of the saving mysteries. She got up and lived a chaste and excellent life in orthodoxy and in all good order, and at the very end of the year she died. The scholasticus Anianus related these wonders to the company of the archimandrite and bishop Father John, Father Julian the presbyter, Father Andrew and Paul, Father Theodore and all their community, when they had been summoned by King Zeno and were on their way to Constantinople.

39. Similar to this account is the story about the blessed Claudian, who was steward over all the property of the church of the city of Eleutheropolis. He was in communion with the bishops, but he had faith in and love for the blessed Father Romanus, and gave many great alms with his monastery, both during his life and after his departure. This man too fell ill, and when he was at his end he was granted a vision and a revelation similar to that one. Immediately, without delay, he ordered his household to take him at night, with no one seeing, and carry him to the monastery of Father Romanus, which was five miles away. When he arrived there, he made his confession to the holy fathers and heads of monasteries who were with Father Leontius, and confessed and related to them the things of the vision. He earnestly entreated them with tears and groans that he might be granted not only the communion of the Orthodox but also the monastic habit. He lived only three days, in all joy and gladness, and then died, and he was laid to rest with the presbyters. This salvation, worthy of wonder, had as its cause the alms that are able to do all things.

40. The blessed Boniface, the Roman presbyter, had such warm zeal against the synod of Chalcedon that he would not receive any of its adherents even in an ordinary matter, nor would he ever even speak with a layman, unless the man first anathematized the synod of Chalcedon, even if he only met him on the road. This was especially because he had seen a vision like this. When the iniquity took place, he seemed to see a dead man laid on a bier before the holy Anastasis, who stank greatly and filled the air with his stench. This man quietly came to life and was about to reign, and he held a book in his hand. He gave it to the presbyter Boniface, saying, "Take this book from me." On the outside it was splendidly adorned, but when he took it from him and opened it, he found it full of worms inside. This signified that although Nestorius was dead, he lived on through Juvenal, who became the heir of that man's stinking glory. The blessed Father Peter also said that the wretched Juvenal had filled the Church with negligent people to such an extent that something like this happened in his days. At that time Father Peter was living in quiet in the holy city.

41. A certain Bessian deacon, while he was keeping the day of his service at the holy Anastasis and the shrine of the holy martyrs, had intercourse with a woman. Then he went in to sleep, as was his custom, inside the holy place of Golgotha in the upper room, on the bed that had been spread there, since it was summer. While the doors were locked, a voice came: "Oh, how much impurity has filled my house, Juvenal! They have defiled it. Throw this leper outside!" In the morning, with the doors still locked, he was found in the street in front of the shrine of the holy martyrs, lying on the bed and being mocked. When many people came running, he woke up and realized his shame. He became penitent and told everyone his sin with tears. Fear and trembling seized everyone at what had happened. And so Juvenal, as though acting out of piety, removed him from the service. For this reason the Father said of the blessed Gerontius the deacon, who was then of the monastery of the blessed Melania, that whenever he was going to perform the evening service there, he fasted two days at a time.

42. This Juvenal, before the synod of Chalcedon, wanted to make the blessed Father a chartularius, while he was living in quiet in his cell in the holy city, beside the Tower of the patriarch David. Since the blessed one realized this, he guarded himself and did not go out anywhere. But when there was an assembly at holy Sion, Juvenal sent men to seize him from his cell, which was nearby, and bring him to him. As the men who had been sent were about to reach his cell, he heard a voice saying to him, "Get up and flee through this little door, for men have been sent after you by Juvenal to take you by force and make you a chartularius." At once he got up and threw himself down from a rather high roof, and with the help of the Lord, who helped and kept him, he landed upright on his feet. Escaping in this way, he fled from their hands. From that day on he refused to assemble with that impious man.

43. In the region of Ascalon there was a woman, the blessed Mika, who lived to the age of a hundred. She lived and conducted herself in asceticism, in all chastity and in the fear of God, and she had experience of God's grace. Through it she was fully assured about the iniquity that took place at the synod of Chalcedon. She declared it before everyone, and she blessed those who did not enter into communion with it and confirmed them. And she saw Satan openly threatening her with death and saying to her, "Why do you dare to make people stumble over the great synod and slander it?" Old as she was, he threw her from the bench on which she had been placed, and he persisted for a long time, fighting with her, until she grew strong in faith, took dust, and threw it at him in the name of the Lord. In this way she drove him off, so that he no longer dared to come near her. Father Theodore the presbyter related this to us. At times he conversed with her and received some of her excellence and holiness.

44. The blessed Urbicia the deaconess was the daughter of one of the bishops of Crete. When her father died, she loved Christ and renounced the world with her brother, the blessed Euphrasius. She took up the complete renunciation of the world, by which I mean exile: she left her city and came to the holy city with her brother. They bought a monastery near the holy place of the Ascension and lived there in quiet, practising asceticism well and persevering in the service of God. Some time later the holy bishop Epiphanius of Pamphylia, after the overturning of the Encyclical, refused to go along with those other bishops in the overturning. So it happened that he was driven out of his church in Pamphylia and went into exile. He came to the holy city and was received by them, and with them he lived in quiet and asceticism, as an example for everyone, and for their confirmation and edification. But the Accuser envied this and stirred up a persecution against them, in this way. The administrator of Jerusalem at that time sent the archdeacon of the Ascension with some other men to rebuke them. When he came to them and saw their excellence, he advised them as a man close to them, saying, "Enter into communion with the bishop, and you will keep your monastery, your quiet and his love." The blessed woman said, "How can we break the covenant we made with Christ and enter into communion with the synod of Chalcedon?" He said, "Enter into communion at my risk, and this sin will not be yours." The blessed woman turned to him and said, "Tell me, my lord father, how much is your risk worth, that I should buy the salvation of my soul with such a thing? So listen. Even if the saints Enoch, Noah and Daniel were to come and advise me to enter into communion with you, and even if a voice came from heaven above saying to me, 'Be persuaded by them and enter into communion with them,' I would never consent to do it, unless my father Timothy, the holy monk who handed down to me the orthodox faith in Crete, were himself to come to life, come here, and release me from the judgment and the anathema he laid on me." Whoever has ears to hear, let them hear! Since they were found worthy to suffer and be persecuted for Christ with the holy Epiphanius, and the monastery was taken from them along with the goods that were in it, they wove the crown of confession and went to Alexandria. There they were received with honour by the Orthodox clergy, monks and laity, and in many ways they glorified God and were glorified by him. Later they returned to Maiuma of Gaza, and there they completed the course of their confession and died. And she, the God-clad, blessed prophetess, full of every grace of the Holy Spirit, died in the body but lives in the spirit; and, to speak truly, having chosen the good portion, she has her dwelling in heaven.

45. The blessed Father told us about two holy men, aged Cilician monks, Torquatus and Hermogenes, who went up to the court in his days. They told him that Theodore of Mopsuestia, the wicked heretical bishop of the two natures, who together with Diodore was the teacher of Nestorius, was so defiant toward God that he would do away with the epistles contained in the Acts of the Apostles, and with the Gospel of John, as though on his own authority. "When we went in to him and reproached him," they said, "he rebuked us, saying that it is not for monks to pry into such matters, and so he dismissed us with insults. Three days later he went mad and began eating his own flesh, and he died." After the Encyclical, many holy monks everywhere, by the power and grace of Christ, refused to go along with its overturning. Instead, inflamed with divine zeal, they stood firm in the true faith and confession.

46. A sign like this took place in Pamphylia. Some monks who agreed with these two-nature bishops were cutting wood in the forests, and they got into a quarrel with Orthodox monks, examining the faith and arguing about it. Both sides decided to hold a trial by fire and to take its judgment. So they threw into a blazing pyre the Encyclical of the true faith, and the definition of faith of the synod of Chalcedon together with the Tome of Leo, and waited to receive God's judgment. Immediately, without delay, as soon as the fire touched the Definition and the Tome of Leo, they turned to ash and dust. But the divine Encyclical was preserved without blemish and without harm in the middle of the fire. For this reason those who belonged to the communion of the deniers repented and turned away from their error, and taking up zeal for the fear of God, they became Orthodox.

47. And if anyone does not believe this wonder, to which God is witness, here is one like it, as the blessed Basilides, a chosen monk, related to us. He said that something like this happened in a village near Ptolemais, where the monastery of Father Claudian is. In that time of denial, Claudian was zealous, a champion and leader in the struggle for the orthodox faith. This is what happened. The presbyter of that village was disputing about the faith with one of its inhabitants, a layman, but orthodox and zealous for the faith, and was pressing him either to enter into communion with him or to leave the village. With all the villagers standing around, the presbyter challenged that orthodox man, saying, "Do you want to find out which of us believes rightly? Let us light a fire, and you and I will put our right hands into it. Whoever's hand is preserved unharmed, it will be known that the orthodox faith is with him." The layman said, "I am a layman and a sinner, and you are a presbyter. How can I contend with you in this?" But the villagers standing there praised the proposal, clapped their hands, and urged that it be done. The orthodox man agreed. At once a great deal of wood was gathered, and the flames rose high. The villagers bound the hands of both men with cloths, brought them up to the fire, and they touched it. The presbyter's hand was immediately, without delay, completely burned, but the hand of the believing orthodox layman remained unharmed. The blessed monk Basilides confirmed this to us: "At that time I was an oil merchant, and while I was selling oil in those parts I was granted to converse with that confessor. I stayed with him, and I was delighted and strengthened."

48. Hear also of a wonder like this one, which happened in a village of Saltus called Aphtha, near which is the monastery of the holy Silvanus, father of monks. A monk lived there named Epiphanius, chaste, humble and meek in his simplicity, who held fast to the true faith from his youth. He had received it from holy fathers and orthodox monks, I mean from the blessed Tatian and Maron, who were of his own people. But the Enemy, who is envious and does wicked things, envied the salvation of these men and stirred up against them the presbyter of the village, a violent and quarrelsome man. He saw that this man alone had separated from his church and was not in communion with him or with the people of the village; the villagers, it seems, had been slandering him to the presbyter. So he summoned him and threatened him with blows, insults and banishment after the next day: he would suffer all these things unless he came and entered into communion with him. But the poor orthodox man said to him, "It is impossible for me to betray my faith, which I received from the holy fathers." When he was let go, he prepared himself for flight, so as to offer his exile to God, showing God the oppression he was under and the affliction he suffered for His name's sake. But the next day that presbyter, who was healthy and had nothing wrong with him, died. As a result all the inhabitants of the village were afraid and astonished at what had happened, and they left the orthodox Epiphanius alone and no longer pressed him. Having received the beautiful crown of zeal from a righteous judgment, he was granted to fall ill in the coenobium of our holy and blessed father Isaiah, where he used to receive the mysteries. When he died there, he was buried in the church among the saints, in a tomb where he lies alone.

49. After the visitation, the Father moved from Maiuma and was in Alexandria. There he was taken in by one of those who love strangers and love the saints, and he was hidden from most people. At that time Father Pior, father of monks, a prophetic man renowned everywhere, heard a voice saying to him, "Get up and go down to the city of Alexandria. When you go in to bishop Peter the confessor, who has been banished and is hiding there, comfort him and strengthen him, and rejoice with one another." Father Pior said, "Who will show me the place where he is?" The voice said to him, "Set out on the road and do not worry." So he got up at night and came to the city. When he entered the gate, he saw a pillar of fire guiding him, not only through the street but right into the courtyard, and up the staircase through its many floors, until he reached the place where the holy Peter was. Father Pior went up and knocked at the door. The blessed one was afraid to open to him, because he did not know who he was. Father Pior said, "Do not be afraid, Father Peter. It is I, poor Pior. The Lord has sent me to you." So he opened the door and received the saint, and they rejoiced with each other and were greatly comforted. It happened that the master of the house had an infant, a little child not yet baptized, and he begged the Father to baptize him. The blessed one excused himself, since he had no suitable place, and the people who should assist him in the service were not near. But the man persisted, pressing and entreating him, until the blessed one was compelled to keep the door shut and not open it. Then something happened that God knows: when the door was opened, the child was found in front of the saint, crawling and rolling about. The saint was greatly amazed at this, and being persuaded that it was God's will, he agreed to baptize him. No one was with him except Father Pior, who happened to be present then, and he was not a cleric but a layman. Even so, out of necessity he asked him to hold the infant above the basin, so that he could pour the water. When Pior came to hold him, he saw the grace of the priesthood above the head of the blessed one, and he was afraid and fled, crying out, "Ubsais, Ubsais!", which means "My lord, my lord!" The blessed one held the child himself, and with difficulty persuaded him to take part with him in the holy act, saying to him, "Do not fear judgment as one unworthy, for this is happening out of necessity, according to the will of God, so that this believer, the lover of strangers who has received us, may be granted your blessing and the grace that comes from God."

50. Once this Father Pior, while in a vision, saw a great crowd of monks carrying one large cross on their shoulders, holding it by both ends, with their backs turned toward each other. Some were pulling this way and others the opposite way, and they were hindering one another and being hindered by one another. This signified the schism that has now arisen in the quarrel and struggle between the Orthodox monks of Egypt and of Palestine, both sides believing that they were contending for the truth out of great zeal and earnestness. One of the ancient saints, Father Lucius of the Cells, foreseeing this in the Spirit, also made it known, saying to those with him, "If any of you live long enough, you will reach a time when two will be arrested to bear witness for Christ and for orthodoxy, and yet will not be in communion with each other."

51. In the same way, the blessed Urbicia, whom we mentioned above, saw a fearful vision that signified this. She saw herself going up at night to the holy Ascension, as was her custom, to worship alone in quiet. When she bowed down on the steps, she saw in the portico in front of the church of the holy Ascension a woman clothed in purple garments and shining with [?]. Trembling with fear, she fell on her face and lay on the ground. But the holy Theotokos, for it was she, came up and raised her, saying, "Do not be afraid, mother. Do not be alarmed." She took her by the hand and walked with her, and in her radiance she looked down from the portico, gazing at the mountain. She said to mother Urbicia, "Handmaid of God, do you see what the mountain is like? It appears to you at a time like this; tell me how you see it." She said, "I see the whole mountain as though it were made up of splinters of wood." And the Theotokos said, "Just as you see this mountain, so from now on the Church of God will be split apart until the end."

52. Leontius was one of those thought to be of a distinguished and respectable family of Ascalon. In the end he renounced the world and became a monk and an archimandrite. The holy Zeno the desert-dweller prophesied to him: “You will become a bishop, but you will not die a bishop.” So when he became bishop of Ascalon, as the prophecy had said, he was eager to win the friendship and confidence of the heretic Nestorius, who then held the church of Constantinople. Leontius was a man full of hypocrisy and worldly thinking. That is why, when the wicked Nestorius was in exile, he sent him honours and gifts in his exile. Later, when the synod of Chalcedon took place, he went up to it too, and people used to say that he was the one who, more than anyone else, urged Juvenal to raise his hand in the denial. When the people of Ascalon learned this, they were zealous for the faith and got ready not to receive him when he came back, but either to drive him out or to stone him. So when he returned and was kept out of Ascalon by night, he knew the zeal of its people and turned back to Cyprus. When he died there, his people took his body and hurried to bring it secretly to Ascalon and bury it there by night. A ship was found sailing from Constantinople, and they put him on board. Now that ship was also carrying the body of a charioteer who came from Ascalon. He had been summoned to Constantinople and had won fame there for his skill. When he died, his people embalmed him in honey, laid him in a lead coffin and were bringing him home to his family. A fierce storm came up at sea and a tempest arose, putting everyone on board in danger of death. The sailors began bringing out the cargo and throwing it overboard to lighten the ship. Along with everything else they decided to throw out the charioteer’s body too and keep only the bishop’s, out of respect for the episcopal office. But the justice of God was guiding events, and in their haste amid the tempest and storm the sailors threw the body of Leontius into the sea in place of the charioteer. When they had sailed on and reached Ascalon, they quietly sent for Leontius’s household, who took the body by night before anyone in the city knew and hurried to bury it. When they opened the coffin to bury the body, they found the charioteer in all his gear: a helmet on his head, his whip in his hand, and his straps bound around him. They were astonished, and they ordered those standing nearby not to let anyone know anything. They carried the charioteer to his grave as though it were the body of Bishop Leontius. People said, though, that the charioteer had been a good man who loved to give alms and kept the commandments. In this way the prophecy of the holy Zeno was fulfilled. I have heard these things confirmed by many others as well. The God-fearing father Zachariah the priest used to tell about Zosimus, one of the leading men of Ascalon, that he had told him about it and confirmed that he had witnessed it himself and was fully convinced. For he was a kinsman of Leontius, and since he was one of the people secretly called to the burial, he saw these things and bore witness to them.

53. The father said: “Three years before the synod of Chalcedon took place, I was in Jerusalem with the blessed Theodotus and some of the fathers. About the seventh hour of the day all of us plainly saw three suns in the sky: one in the east, one in the west and one in the middle of the sky. God alone knows what power and vision this was. Still, it surely pointed to how the matter would turn out.”

54. The father said: “I was in Egypt at the time when the blessed Theodosius, archbishop of Jerusalem, was perfected in martyrdom for the truth at Constantinople. That very night I saw him rising up to heaven wrapped in a white stole, the kind the bishops of Jerusalem usually wear when they baptize. It shone and flashed until he entered heaven. I took note of the day, and later, when news of his death arrived, I found that it was the same day on which I had seen that vision.”

55. There are those who say to us: “The whole world takes communion in the churches. You alone, a small number, separate yourselves, and you call yourselves orthodox and zealots for the truth.” The fathers have handed down to us that we should answer them like this. Remember how many tens of thousands, all of them together, were rebellious and transgressors and perished in the wilderness. Not only did they lose the everlasting good things, but their wrongdoing kept them out of the land of promise. That lawgiver and great prophet Moses also warned them: “You shall not follow the many in doing evil.” Again, in Persia, when all the captives of Judah bowed down to the king’s image, these three youths held firm, refusing to bow and refusing to transgress. Because of this, they praised God and were praised by him in return. They also brought the king and the many who were there at the time to the true knowledge of God. With whom, then, do you want to share and have your portion? With Joshua son of Nun, Caleb son of Jephunneh and those three youths in Babylon, or with the whole world that bowed down to the golden image? Think about this when it comes to the great crowd at Chalcedon, at the synod of the deniers. The priestly saying of Jeremiah the prophet fits it all the better: “Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard and defiled my inheritance; they have made my desirable portion a desolation that no one treads.” And again: “Better is one who does the will of the Lord than a thousand.”

56. When the denier Juvenal came back from the synod of the wrongdoers, the holy orthodox fathers and the monks in Palestine decided to meet him on the road. They meant to do all they could to persuade him to recognize his folly, correct himself and remove the stumbling block from the world. They also urged the blessed Abba Peter, who was then living at [?] of Maiuma, to go with them. At first he declined, because he was not in the habit of leaving the place, and because of the business with worldly men and the crowd from Constantinople, for Juvenal had many of them coming down with him to help and guard him. Then the Saviour appeared to him and said: “I am being wronged and my faith is being violated, and you are looking after your own honour and your quiet?” This moved him, and he got up and set out, and all of them went eagerly, as though going to bear witness. When the fathers met the impious Juvenal, the blessed Theodosius spoke up. He was a monk from among the faithful who later became archbishop of Jerusalem. He boldly rebuked Juvenal for the denial at Chalcedon, since he had been present the whole time and knew everything that had been done, and he exposed Juvenal’s hypocrisy and denial. Juvenal grew angry and ordered a certain man, a [?], one of those around him, to deal carefully with this man as a troublemaker who was opposing the will of the emperor. When that man was about to do this, the blessed Peter blazed with zeal. He was still only a monk at the time and did not hold the rank of bishop, but he knew by the power of prophecy what kind of man this was. He said: “You dare to put yourself forward in a matter of faith, or to speak at all? Did you not commit fornication upon fornication this very night? I am the least of all the saints here. Do you want me to speak, so that fire comes down from heaven at once and consumes you and those around you?” Then the man was seized with fear and trembling and realized who Peter was. He fell at his feet and begged him in front of everyone: “Forgive me, my lord [?]. I did not know your holiness was here.” So he let the blessed Theodosius go and no longer dared to say anything more or to attack the saints. Then he took Juvenal and went back to Caesarea.

57. Abba Paul the Apospistos [?], who was a fellow solitary of the old man Abba Andrew the desert-dweller, told us: “At the time of the synod of Chalcedon there were two of us living in solitude, I and my brother, whose name was Eusebius. He was an eloquent man and very learned in worldly wisdom. He was in doubt about the doctrine of the two natures and kept begging the Lord to receive assurance from his grace about how to think on this and whom to follow: those who refuse to speak of two natures, or those who accept them. Then the holy John the Evangelist appeared to him and said: ‘Eusebius, that which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which was revealed to us, which we have seen with our eyes and our hands have touched: the Word of life.’ Having been convinced and strengthened in this way, he became a herald of the truth.”

58. A certain Anianus was a priest and steward of the holy church in Jerusalem. After the denial he withdrew. Being a zealous orthodox man, he told the blessed Abba Peter and Abba Stephen the priest about the synod held at Ephesus, where the wicked Nestorius was rejected. He had gone up there with Juvenal, and from that time on he saw great hypocrisy in him. He said Juvenal was ready to betray the faith and would have done so if he had not been openly put to shame by the blessed Cyril, and afraid of his fervent zeal and boldness. After that Anianus no longer wanted to receive the offering from Juvenal’s hands, since he regarded him as a hypocrite and a transgressor.

59. Those who fell at Chalcedon may say to us: “On what grounds do you call us transgressors or wrongdoers?” We answer them that there is an apostolic law which says: “For if I build up again the things I tore down, I show myself to be a transgressor.” At Ephesus you rejected Nestorius, the head of the two natures. In doing so you tore down the very teaching that two natures should be spoken of, and you anathematized those who had dared, or would dare, to think or teach this. How then are you not guilty and transgressors? For the very things you tore down then, you built up again at Chalcedon, out of human fear, love of ease and the urging of the wicked emperor. You also received the wicked Theodoret and Ibas without a trial, though they had been condemned and deposed for this very impiety. You fell into this kind of transgression not just once, but twice, three, four and five times, tearing down the impiety and building it up again. How, you ask? At the synod of Ephesus you tore down this wicked doctrine, and then you built it up again at Constantinople, with the two divided natures. A little later, at the second synod held at Ephesus, the pious and orthodox patriarch Dioscorus presided, and you, Juvenal, together with the assembly of orthodox bishops, tore down the impiety. A short time after that you openly built it up again at the synod of Chalcedon. And, as I said before, you received Theodoret and Ibas without a trial, men who had been deposed for this impiety. Again, in the Encyclical issued in the days of the blessed Archbishop Timothy, you rejected this same impiety by a general, worldwide renunciation. A little later you built it up again in what is called the Antiencyclical. In this you fulfilled what Jeremiah the prophet said: “They have loved to wander with their feet, and they did not spare the One who is.” You have become a reed shaken by the wind, blown about and tossed by every wind, forever limping on both legs and never standing firm on the way of truth. Concerning you it is written: “I hate those who commit transgression.” And God declares about such people through Isaiah the prophet at the end of his book: “You will go out and see the corpses of the men who transgressed against me. Their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched, and they will be a horror to all flesh.” But these are not the only reasons you are, and are called, transgressors. You also transgressed the definition of the first synod of Ephesus, which deposed Nestorius. It decreed that no one, whether bishop or cleric, is permitted any longer to put forward, set out, write or compose any other creed or teaching about the faith beyond the one first set forth by the three hundred and eighteen bishops with the Holy Spirit. Those who dare to do anything of this kind are to be removed: bishops from the episcopate and clerics from the clergy. Those assembled at Chalcedon certainly knew this definition. At first they at once stood up, unwilling to introduce any such novelty, and cried out with loud voices: “Let no one make another creed! We will not attempt it, and we do not dare. The fathers have taught. What they set forth is enough. We cannot say or think or set forth anything beyond it. No one has authority to make another creed. There is a canon which says that what has been set forth is enough.” Many other such things are written in the minutes of that time, which expose and shame their hypocrisy and transgression. More than that, they show that these men must be anathematized by us. Another apostolic canon commands: “Whoever preaches to you anything other than what we preached to you, let him be anathema.” And again: “Even if I, Paul, or an angel from heaven should preach to you anything other than what you have received, let him be anathema.” So they preached to us something beyond the Gospel and contrary to what we received from the synod of the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers, and above all from the synod at Ephesus, which deposed Nestorius and rejected the doctrine of the two natures. Those assembled at Chalcedon wickedly preached another, new creed. By this they became liable to the apostolic anathema, and they are justly anathematized by all who fear God. So we do not anathematize them on our own authority or by our own judgment. We hold fast to the apostolic canons and the definitions of the holy fathers, and so for us they are transgressors and anathematized.

60. A God-fearing man once saw in a vision an assembly of all the bishops, with the holy Paul the apostle standing among them. Paul cried out: “These are my injunctions to you. These are the covenants I established for you. These are my commandments.” After he had explained them, he said to them: “Come, wash your faces in this basin.” For a basin full of water had been set down in their midst. When they washed, the faces of all of them turned out to be leprous. And he said to them: “So not one of you has been found clean.”

61. I hear that one of the saints spoke boldly before the wicked Marcian. Rebuking the doctrine of the two natures, he told him plainly and in a holy manner: “I was close to Christ and went about with him everywhere. He worked wonders, healed and taught. He was hungry and was persecuted. He was arrested, scourged, crucified and suffered. He was buried, rose again, ascended and sat down at the right hand of his Father. Through all of it I was with him. The one I saw teaching, healing and raising the dead is the very same one I saw growing weary, weeping, hungering and thirsting, and enduring those other sufferings. Never did I see two in him, one and then another. Always it was the same one who did these things and those, who suffered and was glorified: the one nature of God the Word incarnate.” The wicked emperor was amazed at the man and put to shame, and he dismissed him with honour and in peace.

62. Again, another servant of Christ named John, a comes [?] among the believers in Alexandria, was arguing with a colleague [?] of his who was one of the Syrian Nestorians and was wickedly sunk in the error of the two natures. John said to him: “Do you confess that the holy Virgin is the Mother of God?” The man replied: “I confess that she is Mother of God and Mother of Christ.” John answered him: “So what did she bear, two or one?” Under this pressure his mouth was stopped. Those standing nearby and listening were amazed, and they praised God for the wisdom given to his servant on behalf of the truth.

63. Abba John the bishop, who is called “of the Diaconia,” archimandrite of the monastery in Egypt and a holy and wise man, always used to say this about the synod of Chalcedon: that it is the voice of the Jews, who said to Christ: “Why do you, being a man, make yourself God, making yourself equal to God?”

64. In Pamphylia a layman named Marcian, a zealous orthodox man, rebuked the bishop of the city in front of the congregation, because he was expounding the faith wickedly. He was arrested by the governor and given severe, cruel blows on his back and belly, almost to the point of death. He was carried home in that state and was thought to have died. Yet the next day he was found with no injury at all. He told the faithful: “After three lashes I saw a man dressed in white garments standing at my right. From then on I no longer felt the blows. It was as if papyrus was brushing against me.” There was also a man who had suffered for many years from a severe, incurable itch. He took some of the blood that had flowed from Marcian’s body in faith, washed with it, and was at once cleansed of his ailment.

65. While our father, the blessed Abba Peter, was serving as bishop in his church at Maiuma, Abba Isaiah the solitary, who was then shut up in his cell, saw this vision. There was a huge, high, foul heap of filth in the middle of the dwelling-place. It took up almost the whole place, and its stench drove many people away. An angel came down from heaven holding a basket and said to Abba Peter the bishop: “Take this shovel from me and clean the stench out of the dwelling-place, for you have been commanded to clear it.” The saint declined, saying: “I cannot do this. The task is beyond my strength; in fact, I say it is beyond human strength altogether.” But the angel did not stop pressing him until he had made him lift the basket to clean the dwelling-place. When Abba Isaiah had seen these things, he left his cell at daybreak and came to the blessed man at Maiuma. When they had seen each other and exchanged blessings, he told him this vision and then went back to his cell. What this vision meant is known only to God, who alone is wise and knows everything hidden. But it surely points to the time to come. 65. The blessed Timothy, archbishop of Alexandria and confessor, was in exile when Abba John was sent to him by the orthodox fathers in Palestine and by Abba Peter the bishop to visit and comfort him. Timothy told him: “When the synod of Chalcedon assembled, I saw in a vision that a congregation was gathering in the church of Alexandria. When I went up to take the offering, all that was there was black bread and sour wine.” This signified the abandonment by the grace of God that was to come upon the churches.

66. The same man, Archbishop Timothy, also told this: “When the blessed Dioscorus was about to leave for the synod, I saw a vision like this. The blessed Dioscorus was going into the martyr’s shrine of the holy John the Baptist to take his leave before setting out and to receive his prayer. After the prayer he went up the steps to take his seat, as is the custom. Once he sat down, the whole clergy turned away from him and left him, and only I stayed by him. While I was standing by him, a great, ferocious wolf came at us. It leapt on the holy Dioscorus, seized him by the neck and began biting him. But it had no teeth, so it did him no harm. Then I saw a soldier appear, and he killed the wolf at once.” It is clear that the wolf was Proterius.

67. Archbishop Timothy also told this: “At that time I dreamed that I saw a wild, savage horse kicking with its hooves and throwing the dwelling-place into turmoil. Everyone else ran away from it. I alone took heart and confronted it, and when I had overcome it by the power of God, I tied it up and shut it in a cell, and it was never seen again.” This was the wicked Marcian, and his death by the wrath of God.

68. He also told another vision, which Proterius himself had interpreted for him when Timothy was serving as a cleric under him at that time: “I dreamed I saw a tyrant come into the church and fight with everyone. Some he struck, some he chased, some he killed, and others he brought into subjection. I was filled with zeal and could not bear such insolence and violence. The Lord gave me strength, so I took courage, went up to him, rebuked him and drove him out of the church. The next day I was telling the vision to the clergy, and Proterius himself, who was standing nearby, spoke up and said: ‘After the holy Dioscorus a heretic will seize the churches. You will drive him out and become bishop in his place.’”

69. That same Proterius used to tell of one of the holy women. When the deposition and exile of the blessed Dioscorus became known in Alexandria, she said that the man who came after Dioscorus was the Antichrist. So she rebuked Proterius for these things to his face, and after suffering much at his hands she put on the crown of the confessors.

70. My brother, the blessed Evagrius, was in communion with the bishops when he left Berytus with Zachariah, Anatolius and Philip to renounce the world. He came to Tyre to Abba Elijah the priest and was persuaded there of the true faith. The next day he was to anathematize the synod of Chalcedon and receive communion from him. That night he saw in a dream that his tongue had an ulcer [?], like some old, foul, festering itch. At once he spat it out and woke up. The next day, as I said, when he was about to receive communion and anathematize the synod, he remembered his dream: the foul itch stood for the stench of the two natures.

71. So he grasped the meaning of the dream. Brother Anastasius, a monk from Edessa who had been a scholasticus, had a similar experience. While he was still in Berytus and taking communion with the deniers, he saw a holy, venerable old man, who said to him: “If you want to be saved, take a horse and hurry to Bishop Peter the Iberian. From him you will receive the true seal and be saved.” Anastasius said: “At once I shook off everything and came to the father, who was then at Aphthorida [?] with Abba Gregory.” He told Peter what he had seen in the vision, along with many other things he had seen while he was in Antioch and on his way up. These had already shown him earlier that he ought to withdraw from the world, and they were calling him to change his life and leave this world completely. He was persuaded, made his request and was received by Peter, and was instructed in the true faith. After anathematizing the synod of Chalcedon he became a monk under him and withdrew from the world. He told us that the night before he was to receive communion, “I dreamed I saw myself like someone newly baptized, wearing a shining stole, with many people walking ahead of me carrying candles. I was puzzled and kept wondering how this could happen to me, since I had already been baptized once, as a child. Then I saw the old man I had seen in Berytus. He said to me: ‘Do not be afraid or doubt. This is not a second baptism. Everyone who becomes orthodox is granted light like this, and glory and splendour.’”

72. The same vision was seen by Gaïon, a lover of Christ, who was one of the senior officers on the governor’s staff. He came from Sebaste in Palestine, where the body of the holy John the Baptist lies. He met the blessed Peter the bishop, was instructed by him and received the precise teaching of the orthodox faith. When he was about to anathematize the synod of Chalcedon and enter into communion with the saints, he saw himself in a night vision dressed in white, with many people walking ahead of him, as they do before someone newly baptized, carrying torches and lights. Persuaded in this way, he broke off communion with the estranged and became an orthodox and zealous man.

73. The scholasticus Zachariah from Maiuma was orthodox, very zealous and precise in matters of doctrine, so much so that he was able to help others as well. While he was in Berytus, he saw himself as though he were in the church of those who are in communion there. As the congregation was coming to the end of the service and the deacons were giving the cup, they did not say any holy or mystical word. They said something else instead, shameful and indecent. He was troubled and alarmed, and then he saw Abba Isaiah, the father of monks, whom he knew, for he had seen him many times. Isaiah said to him: “Flee from the church of these Tetradites and separate yourself from them.”

74. A God-loving priest of the Alexandrians named Theamison, a man renowned for his chastity and modest way of life, told us: “When Salofaciolus held the church of Alexandria, I was serving the church of Naracrura [?] at that time. I had charge of the diaconicon and was entrusted with the vessels of the service, and because of the troubles I stayed there and slept there. The bishop of that city had been driven out by the citizens as a heretic. When Salofaciolus went there, he brought him along so that he could return and take over the church. As I said, I had charge of the diaconicon, so I intended to wait for his arrival, hand over every one of the vessels to him first, and so escape slander and harassment. That night, as I slept in the diaconicon, I saw many companies of saints dressed in white, and the holy Mother of God standing among them. She was hurrying to leave that place. A donkey was brought, as it seemed, beautifully and modestly saddled, and she sat on it while the saints lifted her up. As she was about to go out, with the saints going ahead of her, she looked at me from where she sat on the donkey and beckoned to me with her hand. She called me and said: ‘Get out of here. Do not stay. Follow me.’” So this man, holding letters of priesthood, came at once to Alexandria. The orthodox fathers came to love him dearly. When the holy bishop Timothy returned, Theamison found great favour with him, as a chosen orthodox man adorned with other virtues as well. Timothy kept him there, and he stood victorious in the faith to the end. Both while the blessed Timothy was still alive and after he fell asleep, he gathered the people, strengthening and building them up until his last breath.

75. He also told this: “As I said, that heretic bishop was about to come to Naracrura [?]. All of us orthodox clergy decided to leave before he arrived. One of the townspeople had an infant who was not yet baptized, and he begged to have the child baptized by the orthodox before the heretic arrived and he was put under pressure. When the baptism was completed, the baby who had just been baptized cried out: ‘Catch it, catch it, this dove that is flying away and escaping!’” It was the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove. This made it plain that once heretics seize the churches, the grace of the Holy Spirit departs and abandons them.

76. The father told us: “At the time when Proterius was in Alexandria, I was living in the harbour of the city of Jamnia. I had a friend there, a cleric, who at first was considered orthodox and zealous. In the end he went into communion with Proterius and [?], and became steward of the church’s affairs, carrying himself with great pomp. Once, when I was hurrying to visit one of the saints, I ran into him in a narrow spot in the city as he was going along in procession. When I saw him I wanted to hide, but I could find no place to hide, so I turned my face to the wall. But he saw me and recognized me, ran up to me and greeted me. I was flustered and caught off guard at the same moment, so I answered and greeted him and said, ‘Bless me.’ He said to me: ‘Why are you running away from me? Am I not your friend? What wrong have I done, that you turned away from me?’ All I said to him was, ‘You know what you have done,’ and I walked past him. That very night I saw a great plain full of light and heavenly glory, with companies of saints and ranks of angels praising and glorifying God, and the Lord himself in their midst. When I saw him I ran to worship him. I hurried, feeling sure in my mind that I knew him well and could approach him freely. But when he saw me coming toward him from far off, he turned his face away from me in displeasure, in front of all the saints, so that all the saints were astonished. I immediately understood the reason: it must have been that meeting, that encounter with the denier which had befallen me. I fell down in tears and said: ‘Lord, have mercy on me. You know, Knower of hearts, that I did it neither wholeheartedly nor willingly; I did it because I was caught off guard and flustered.’ Then all the saints pleaded on my behalf, and he was moved to receive me.”

77. Our father also told us this about Serapion the scholasticus. He was a deeply faithful man, zealous for orthodoxy, a lover of the saints, and the leading scholasticus in Alexandria. In the time of Proterius he gave shelter to the saints who were being driven out from every place, and he paid for their keep out of his own earnings. Because of this he was found worthy of a divine vision such as this. The magistrates of Alexandria, to please Proterius, had driven all the orthodox clergy and monks out of the city and out of the monasteries round about, and not one of the saints dared to show himself and offer the oblation for the faithful. When the Lord's feast of Easter, the feast of the whole world, came round, this scholasticus named Serapion was hiding in his house for fear of the heretic. He was in great distress and anguish of soul, as one deprived of the oblation on so holy a day. When the hour of the holy night came, in which they used to hold the holy synaxis, he went out into his courtyard under the open sky and knelt down in tears, praying and pleading with God, his hands stretched out to heaven. As he was praying and about to finish his prayer and lower his hands, a portion of the Lord's body was found in his hand. When he took it, he was so strengthened and confirmed in the faith that he was found worthy to be taken up in chains to Constantinople, after Proterius handed him over to Marcian, and to receive the crown of the confessors. What is more, when he went up to Constantinople he was granted grace and help from our Lord. He appeared so bold before the emperor that he persuaded him to let him live in Constantinople without fear and with freedom of speech, to be counted among the scholastici there and to hold the first rank. And there he died.

78. Some orthodox scholastici of Alexandria were studying in Berytus. Along with others they used to visit a certain stylite [?] who stood in a village near the city. He heard from other people that they did not take communion from the church or from the bishops. He grew angry and said to them, "Where do you take communion, then, since you are in a foreign land?" They answered him boldly, "We have the oblation from our holy orthodox fathers, and we partake of it." He said to them, "And how can this be proper, that you, who are laymen, have persuaded yourselves to take the oblation?" They said to him, "Our fathers, the strict orthodox clergy, persuaded us by all means to do this, as something permitted and fitting." When they returned to Berytus and Sunday came, one of them began to hesitate, remembering the words of that stylite, about whether he should take of that holy oblation by himself. In the end, rebuking himself and strengthened in faith, he approached. When he took the coal, he found in his hand a morsel of blood. This scholasticus himself told us of this miracle, for he later became a monk.

79. The blessed presbyter Stephen, who had been archdeacon in Jerusalem, was a zealous orthodox man. He had a holy sister. During the holy forty days of the fast she used to go whole weeks without food, and through the rest of the year she fasted from one day to the next. She went constantly to the martyrium of Saint Stephen and to that of Saint John the Baptist, and kept vigil there. She reached such a degree of holiness and purity that she saw Saint Stephen and Saint John face to face. They came to her, spoke with her and blessed her. When the synod of Chalcedon took place, she began to doubt whether she should still go to the martyrium as she used to and pray with the wrongdoers, above all with Juvenal the heretic, who then held the church. She was distressed that she would be cut off from the company of the saints. Then Saint Stephen appeared to her and said, "Go in peace to your cell. Do not lose what you gain there, and do not grieve as though you were being separated from us. Wherever you are, we come to you there, and we make our dwelling with you."

80. A certain orthodox woman from Pamphylia renounced the world together with her daughters, came to Jerusalem and lived in stillness on the Mount of Olives. Once she went up to worship at the holy place of the Ascension, and it happened that a synaxis was being held there that day. The doors were shut without her knowing it. Unable to get out, she stood hidden beside a pillar until the synaxis was dismissed, and then she went back to her cell and her daughters. At last she fell sick with the illness of which she died. As her departure drew near, she cried out, "Come and see what accusations they are bringing against me at this hour! They say, 'How can you now be justified, or be counted with the orthodox? When the synaxis was being celebrated by those heretics, you chose to stay and watch the unworthy giving the mysteries to people even more unworthy than themselves.'" Her son, an orthodox man named Theodulus who became a deacon, told us this.

81. He added this as well. Once she saw herself being brought before the throne of God as if for judgment, and she heard a voice coming to her from within the throne: "Do you confess that the Son of God was born of the holy Virgin Mary, the God-bearer? Do you confess that the Son of God was crucified and suffered for us?" After she had confessed this, she was accepted and found worthy of his love for humankind.

82. In Attalia in Pamphylia there was a certain abbess named Zoe, the guide of a monastery of orthodox virgins. She was very pure in her way of life and in her mind, and her ascetic practice was severe. Once, after the reversal of the Encyclical, she fell into a trance and saw herself in paradise, with the tree of life in the middle of it. Many bees were flying about, eager to taste of the tree, but they were not allowed to. They were being driven off by a minister dressed in white who stood by the tree and chased them away with his fan. She asked him why he was driving them away, and he said to her, "Because these are the ones who, after the reversal of the Encyclical, gave their assent to the synod of Chalcedon." Once Claudianus, the bishop of Attalia, came to her, and she reproached him for putting his hand to the so-called Antencyclical. He made excuses, saying, "I signed with my hand, not with my soul or my heart." She said to him, "And how can a hand move unless the soul first wills it and moves it? Can a dead man move? No more can a hand move apart from the soul."

83. Abba Leontius, the desert-dweller from Lycia, was renowned everywhere. When the so-called Antencyclical and the reversal of the orthodox Encyclical were about to take place, he saw in a vision that the altar of the church was being stripped and the holy things were being thrown on the ground. Because of this he testified to everyone, saying, "I will no longer submit to the church of those who worship four gods."
84. At that same time another of the saints saw the church as a kind of stable, full of brute beasts of every kind and a great stench.

85. The blessed Epictetus was archimandrite of the great monastery of the orthodox, and a zealous man, in Pamphylia. Bishop Epiphanius, who was his disciple and successor, told us that once, in a vision, Epictetus saw the bishop of Side, Amphilochius. Amphilochius was reputed to be merciful, and his way of life was blameless and his faith sound; but he had signed the Tome of Leo and taken part in what was done at the synod of Chalcedon. With him was Epiphanius, bishop of Perge. Both were buried in mire up to their necks. Weeping, Father Epictetus said to Amphilochius, "How is it that you, who shone so brightly in a life of virtue, are found in this mire?" He replied, "The good is from God, but the sin is from us. I suffer these things, my lord father, because of the synod of Chalcedon, to which I gave my assent."

86. In Alexandria there was a modest and well-regarded woman named Agathoclea. After the reversal of the Encyclical she was unsure in her own mind where she ought to take communion. She asked the Lord earnestly about this, that he might give her full assurance, and she was heard because of her great modesty. In a vision she saw a great church with two altars in it. The one on the left was shabby and bare, and standing over it, ministering and offering, was a bishop she knew, one of those in communion with the synod of Chalcedon. The other, on the right, was small, but it was adorned and shining with much gold and precious stones. Over it stood a little child offering the sacrifice, and he was the Lord. He said to her, "Take communion from here." Convinced by this, she praised God and kept away from the oblation of the two natures. So she remained orthodox, strict and admirable in life and in faith.

87. In the monastery of Abba Romanus there were two brothers, John and Timothy, who came from Pelusium and belonged to one of the leading families of the city. While the blessed Romanus was still alive they renounced the world and received the monastic habit, so to speak, from his hands. A long time after the death of Abba Romanus, Timothy, one of the two, fell ill with his last sickness. When he died, the brothers took him as is the custom, washed him and laid him on a bier, ready to bury him. But suddenly, out of that stillness, he sat up. Everyone was amazed and astonished, and a great crowd of monks came running together with the abbot of that time. They asked him whether he had truly died, and how he had risen after dying. He said to them, "I truly died. I was carried to the place of judgment and justice and brought before the judgment seat." As he said this he wept bitterly and groaned, and he cried out, "O strictness! O strictness! O strictness! You are my witnesses how careful I was while I was with you not to wound the conscience of any brother, and that I was faithful in everything. Yet none of this enabled me to find mercy and help in that hour and escape torment. I was saved only because I kept the right faith without blemish, and to this very hour have kept my soul, from my youth, far from communion with the heretics of Chalcedon."

88. Something of this kind happened in great Antioch, and I saw it myself. Having experienced it at first hand, I thought it necessary to set it down with what has been written above, for the faith and assurance of many. In that city there is an imperial palace which, as those who have seen them say, is not inferior in beauty, size and all the rest of its splendor to the palaces in Rome and Constantinople. It has long been closed because it is not needed, and is merely kept guarded in case the emperor should happen to come to those parts. By its great gate, the outermost of them all, which is closed as I said, a man came, wearing the humble dress of a layman. He built himself a small hut against that very gate and stayed in it through heat and winter, in cold and nakedness, for he had nothing but a single tunic. He lived in silence and spoke not a word. For many years he stood there, praying with groans and tears. He would take nothing at all from anyone, neither gold nor silver, not even copper coins. But a fuller, his neighbor, who had a shop there, brought him toward evening a little bread and a cooked dish of vegetables or pulses, and some water. When he had taken what he needed, he kept whatever was left over and gave it to the poor who regularly came to him. He set himself before the world as a kind of sign. When I heard these things about him, I was eager to go to him, but I was afraid it might not please the old man and that I would only be troubling him. Nevertheless, calling on our Lord, I went to him. When he saw me, he received me humbly and looked at me with a cheerful face. I saw that he was a man in the middle of old age, gaunt [?] and pale, with a dry face, burned by mourning, tears and ascetic practice. When I had won his favor, I asked him, "Since you love the ascetic life, why did you not choose to live in the desert or in a coenobium, rather than in so splendid and glorious a city? Why have you made your dwelling in the public places of the market, exposed to the open air in this unseemly way?" Without a word he stretched his right hand toward heaven and made known by a sign: "God commanded me." When I asked him why he wept and he gave no answer, I ventured to say to him, "This is what I think: that the time of the end has come, and you have been sent as a witness to us, to proclaim this to the world in this place." He only wept. I went to him many times to learn from his humility, and I profited simply from seeing him, so far as I had the sense to receive correction. He was also orthodox and zealous in the faith. He greatly abhorred the Nestorians and turned his face away from them. In the end, as I heard after I had moved away, he was battered by them with cruel blows, and when he had grown weak from the blows, he died a martyr.

89. At that same time there was a bishop of Qenneshrin named Neon. From his youth he had taken up the yoke of the monastic life and practiced severe asceticism in the great and famous monastery near the city called the monastery of Abba Aqiba, and later he became guide and abbot of that monastery. In the time of Martyrius, the Nestorian bishop who was expelled from Antioch for open heresy, there was much strife in the city. The aforementioned Neon, still an abbot at the time, was zealous: he took the brothers of his monastery, came to Antioch and gave great help to the orthodox, until the heretic Martyrius was driven out of the city. So Peter, who was bishop of the orthodox in Antioch at the time of the Encyclical, wishing to reward him for his zeal and eagerness, made him bishop of Qenneshrin. Since he had always had a great love for me, he heard from me about the old man I mentioned above, who lived beside that palace. When he learned that I knew him, he urged me to take him with me to visit him, so that he might enjoy his company. As we were on our way to him, I said to the bishop, "Wait here a little, while I go ahead and see what the old man is doing, in case he is standing at prayer and we disturb him. I will tell him at once about your God-loving self." When I went on and found him praying, I waited until he had finished. When he had finished, I went in. While I was still speaking with him, Bishop Neon, seeing that I was taking a long time, came up and knocked outside, wanting to come in. I knew it was him, and said to the old man, "This is the one I spoke to you about, my God-loving father. He is knocking." I got up and let the bishop in. The moment he entered, the old man merely looked at his face and was filled with anger. He began to blow in his face again and again, so that I was overcome with embarrassment, and the bishop himself was greatly troubled and put to shame. I kept pleading with the old man and begging him not to do this, saying that this was a bishop, a zealous man who had labored hard for orthodoxy. But he went on blowing at him, stretching out his hand toward him and shaking it in a threatening gesture. He showed great anger and kept saying, "This one! This one!" At last I took the bishop and went out in shame, so as not to trouble the old man any further. I was greatly astonished, and kept wondering why the old man had been so disturbed by Neon and what he could have seen in him. Later, from the way things turned out, I learned the reason. This man, who had been so zealous and ascetic and was reputed to be a champion of the orthodox, in the days of Calendion, that impious and wicked heretic, betrayed the faith and entered into communion with him. He became a grief and a reproach to the orthodox. He went so far in wickedness as to call Christ a man who bore God, and a man who was assumed, and to say that the holy Virgin bore Christ, and to charge [the orthodox] with confusion, mixture and blending in Christ, and other such things. Our orthodox fathers afterwards rejected these expressions. Some of the holy fathers had once used them in simplicity, not to indicate two sons or persons or Christs or natures, but to show the reality and truth of a true and complete incarnation, as we learn from their many writings and treatises. But because of these heretics, who perversely seize on such expressions as though they agreed completely with the wickedness [?] of their doctrine, the orthodox fathers rejected them, as I said. In the same way they also refused to speak of two natures after the union. They also refused to say, when giving the holy things, "The body of Christ" and that phrase alone, but rather "The body of God the Word" and "The body of Christ, God the Word and Savior," as the blessed Cyril taught in his explanation of the eleventh chapter, and as the blessed Timothy did too in the treatise he composed against the Tome of Leo and the synod of Chalcedon. Some of the clergy of Antioch reached such a pitch of wickedness, while the heretic Martyrius still held the church, that they dared to say, when giving the holy things, "The body of the righteous man", that contemptible phrase. Of them the apostle's words may rightly and justly be spoken, which run as follows: "For if anyone who transgresses the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses, how much more severe a punishment do you think he will receive who has trampled on the Son of God, and regarded the blood of his covenant, by which he was sanctified, as that of any man, and has insulted the Spirit of grace?" Fitting too is the word and testimony of God to the whole world, which came from God to the holy Joshua son of Nun, the heir of the authority and the gift of the great Moses. After the great wonders that God worked in Egypt, at the sea and in the desert; after the manna; after many great victories; after the crossing of the Jordan, so worthy of God; after the capture of Jericho and the fall of its walls at nothing but the shout of the people, and its complete destruction and its being placed under the ban; after all these wonders, because of the sin of one man who transgressed God's commandment and took something and stole it from what was under the ban, God was angry with the whole people. Israel was defeated by a few warriors, so that many of them fell, and the whole people was in fear and dread, so that the people lost hope, and so did the great commander Joshua himself. For it is written, "The heart of the people melted and became like water." Let us hear, then, from the account that follows in the holy scriptures, which runs as follows: "Joshua tore his clothes and fell on his face to the ground until evening, he and the elders of the people, and they threw dust on their heads. And Joshua said, 'I ask you, Lord, why did you bring this people across the Jordan, only to hand us over to the Amorites to destroy us? If only we had stayed and lived beside the Jordan! What shall I say, now that Israel has turned its back before its enemy? When the Canaanites and all who live in the land hear of it, they will surround us and wipe us off the earth. And what will you do for your great name?' And the Lord said to Joshua, 'Get up. Why are you lying on your face? The people has sinned and broken my covenant which I established with them. They have stolen from what was under the ban and put it among their own goods. The children of Israel can no longer stand before their enemies, because they have themselves come under the ban. I will be with them no longer unless you cut off the ban from among you.'" If, then, because one man out of that whole people transgressed God's commandment and sinned, great wrath came upon all the children of Israel together, what of the synod of evil name at Chalcedon? There a great many bishops were assembled, and not only an assembly of bishops but also a multitude of the peoples, who were wronged at their hands and led into transgression. And they did not transgress some minor commandment, nor in some worldly matter, but in the very right faith in God and in the confession, which they denied and so came under the ban. For they fell under the anathema of the blessed apostle and of the canons of the holy fathers and of the holy synods that went before. How then could they fail to bring down God's wrath justly on the whole earth? For he says to them now too, "I will be with you no longer unless you remove the ban from among you." The outcome of events has plainly shown this. For behold, from that time the empire of the Romans was brought to nothing and came to its end; from the time when wickedness had its source there, and the abomination called the Tome of Leo went out from it. And that city which was the lady and queen of the whole world was taken captive, and barbarians ruled over her. Over her Jeremiah lamented and said, "How lonely sits the city that was full of peoples!" And again, "The chief of provinces has become a tributary." "The great city, the crown of glory, the joy of the whole earth: all her beauty has been cast away from her. Jerusalem has sinned grievously; therefore she has become a thing to shake at. For the Lord has humbled her for the multitude of her wickednesses, because the ban is among them." Like these laments which the prophet Jeremiah uttered over her in prophecy, Isaiah too says, "How the faithful city Zion has become a harlot! She that was full of justice, and righteousness lodged in her, but now murderers and transgressors of the truth." And to them he says in another place, pronouncing woe on them, "Woe to you, rebellious children! You have made a plan, but not by my hand, and a covenant, but not by my Spirit." For there it was set down, and from there came forth the treasury of all wickedness and blasphemy, the so-called Tome, that is, the letter of Leo. And for this reason God now justly says to them, "I will be with you no longer, because the ban is among you. The children of Israel can no longer stand before their enemies until the ban is taken away from among them." Let us fear, then, that in this transgression committed at the synod of Chalcedon there may be fulfilled the prophecy which the apostle utters: I mean the apostasy after which follows the coming of the Antichrist. The blessed Timothy said this too, the unconquerable champion of the right faith, that pillar of orthodoxy, its guardian and teacher, bishop of Alexandria, who spoke and acted and confirmed by the Spirit of God. He said openly that this is the restraint [?] in which the apostle's word is fulfilled, when the rule of the empire of the Romans is abolished. That never happened at Rome from the time she began to reign until now, when she has sinned a great sin: impiety toward God and denial of him, and the guide of impiety, the so-called Tome of Leo, has gone out from her. This is what we now see and are convinced of. The whole prophecy of the apostle, in the second epistle to the Thessalonians, runs as follows: "We beg you, my brothers, concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering to him, not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed, whether by word or by spirit or by a letter as though from us, saying that the day of our Lord has come. Let no one deceive you in any way. For unless the apostasy comes first and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, the adversary who exalts himself above everything that is called God or is worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God... Do you not remember that I told you these things while I was still with you? And now you know what restrains, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of iniquity is already at work; only he who now restrains will be removed from the midst. And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom our Lord Jesus will consume with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation of his coming. His coming is by the working of Satan, with all power and signs and lying wonders, and with all this deception. God will send them a working of error, so that they believe the lie, so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but took pleasure in iniquity." As for the saying that the mystery of iniquity has already begun to be at work, only he who now restrains will be removed from the midst, the holy fathers and teachers said that it refers in a hidden way to the abolition of the empire of the Romans. Who, then, will be found blessed and thrice-blessed, so firmly established in the faith, so fervent in spirit, so ready for every endurance, and with such boldness, that he can make the apostle's boast, who said, "I have fought the good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept my faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which our Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day"? And he goes on to say, "and not to me only, but also to all who have loved his appearing." For then the prophecy of the prophet Zechariah will be fulfilled, as the Lord's own word and plainly, which says, "And there shall no longer be a ban, nor a Canaanite, in the house of the Lord." Now this is the synod of Chalcedon, with the wickedness of its faith and its new definition. This is the last impious sign and ban, and the first forerunner of the Antichrist, and so are the children of its mystery and those who agree with it in mind. These are the accursed and hateful Canaanites, as we have shown in what was written above. There are also other testimonies, revelations and assurances that came from God, both to the saints in particular and to all people in general, concerning the transgression committed at the synod of Chalcedon. But so as not to make this writing too long, I think these are enough for believing hearers, who, as lovers of God, will gladly receive what has been set down here in all truth. For we shall give account to him who will judge the living and the dead in righteousness, who is the strict judge and knower of hearts, the God of truth. For this reason it is good to keep in this matter, too, the apostle's commandment to Timothy: "You, then, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Jesus Christ. And what you have heard from me before many witnesses, entrust to faithful men who will be able to teach others as well." For to cast the mystery of the fear of God among the unworthy, says Saint Basil, is like pouring precious myrrh into a filthy vessel. The apostle's commandment: "Fight the good fight of the faith; take hold of the eternal life to which you were called, and confessed the good confession before many witnesses. O Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you, and turn away from empty and unclean talk and the contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge, by professing which some have fallen away from the truth. Grace be with you." Amen.
Here end the Plerophories, the testimonies and the revelations that came from God through the saints concerning the heresy of the two natures and the transgression that took place at Chalcedon.

These are the stories that the holy Mar John, disciple of Father Peter the Iberian, the bishop, carefully collected. The holy one.
