I have set down here the stories that show how much harm the Synod of Chalcedon brought in, for it came about through the working of Satan. Next, about a monk who was a deacon. In the city of Edessa there was a church of the holy Mar John the Baptist, which is famous and to this day works wonders. And in that celebrated city there was a custom, kept since ancient times, that anyone who suffered from pain in the eyes would go to that church and stay there to find relief. Now in our own time, four years ago, there was a man from a family of the city of Amida, a modest monk who had been trained in the holy monastery of the Easterners in Edessa, and who is a deacon. This affliction came upon him, a pain in the eyes, although even before this his eyes had been somewhat ailing. So he went out to that church and stayed there day and night. But the pain grew so severe that he fell into utter despair, and in his anguish of heart he wanted to throw himself into the well of water near the church. As he was passing through the door to go, the blessed John the Baptist met him and asked him, "What do you mean to do?" The deacon said, "I am going to throw myself into the well." The saint said to him, "Do not be distressed, and do no harm to yourself." And passing his hand over his face, he said to him, "Go to the water basin and wash, and you will be healed. But do not look for me in this church, for I am not in it, since the Chalcedonians took it over. I no longer enter it; because of their defilement I have departed from it." Then the deacon did as the saint had said, and he was healed.

Let us not doubt these things and say that they are fictions and fabrications. For as before God I tell you that the very persons to whom these things happened are relating them before many people. And you, brother, do not doubt them either, but receive them in all truth and certainty. May the prayer of this faith which we hold save the soul at the last. Let each of us persuade himself to live in the way of life that befits the faith; and if we do this, we shall be found worthy of the kingdom of heaven, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory, and to his Father and his Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen. Again, another story, which took place at Sebaste in Palestine, where the relics of John the Baptist are laid. At the time of the hateful and wicked Synod of Chalcedon there was a paramonarius, Constantine, who served in that blessed place. Every day he delighted in the sight of the Baptist and of Elisha the prophet, and in the familiar boldness he had with the holy John. When the oppression and persecution of Chalcedon came, and the bishops ordained by Athanasius the patriarch were driven out by the wicked Marcian, he was troubled in his thoughts. If he fled from communion with the deniers, he would be cut off from his converse with the holy John the Baptist; but if he stayed, he would be a transgressor. So at the very outset he earnestly entreated the saint to reveal to him what was pleasing to God and would help him. And the Baptist said to him, "Presbyter, do not destroy your soul and deny your faith for my sake. Go out and keep your faith without blemish, and wherever you go, I am with you." So the presbyter went out and remained blameless in exile.

Another story. Persuasive and inspiring like the last, it concerns a vision granted to the God-fearing and holy Rusius [?], a stranger and a modest man. While he was living in a cell on Mount Sinai, he set out and came to Jerusalem, looking for a quiet place, and he arrived at Bethel, where Jacob the patriarch saw the ladder. The paramonarius of that place treated him kindly, urged him at length and pressed him to let him provide a fitting place of rest. But he openly declared, "I cannot do this, because I keep myself apart from the communion and denial of Chalcedon." The paramonarius said to him with oaths, "Not a single [?] will be offered to you in this; only stay with me and sing psalms with me." And in his simplicity his mind inclined to this. That night he saw the patriarch Jacob: a man full of white hair, honorable and venerable, wrapped in a cloak, wearing a [?], and walking about in that place. He came up to him and said, "How is it that you, being Orthodox, share in communion with the deniers, and wish to dwell in this place? Do not betray your faith for my sake. Take care, and flee from communion with the deniers, and you will lack nothing good." And by fleeing he was kept to the end in the Orthodox faith.

Again, another story. As soon as the Orthodox are driven out of their churches, the Holy Spirit departs with them, and [from] whoever goes in to receive communion with the heretics [?]. To confirm this we have related to our hearers a little out of much. A holy man worthy of belief told how there was a holy martyr in the region of the Thebaid who worked wonders and mighty deeds, so that many sick people, demoniacs and lepers came to his church, and he appeared to them face to face. After a time the heretics seized his church, and he would appear on the roads to the sick who were coming to his monastery and say to them, "I am Marcellus [?], the martyr you are going to. Do not go there any more. I am not there; I have departed. Because of the defilement of those who deny God I am no longer seen there." These things are enough for the faithful.
